title: Cal Comes from Behind to Hang on and Beat Virginia Tech, 25-20 - Write For California
content: Cal (3-3) and Virginia Tech (4-2) met for the third time this afternoon, and the conference foes have developed an affinity for one another that has, in recent history, translated into odd games. Today kept that tradition alive. The first quarter was scoreless and featured little of note, except for a Hokies field goal attempt that sailed wide left. Standout Cal safety Kingston Lopa and QB1 Jaron Keawe-Sagapolutele were both out after sustaining concussions in last week’s game against UNLV. Virginia Tech broke the seal three minutes into the second quarter, when QB Ethan Grunkemeyer found WR Ayden Greene for a 30-yard touchdown. After little to that point in the game, the Bears answered with their first successful drive later in the quarter, highlighted by a 42-yard shot to Chase Hendricks and another 23-yarder to Jordan King. Ashten Emory, starting in place of Adam Mohammed, scored a few plays later to even the score at 7-7 with six minutes left in the half. Write For California is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Penalties have plagued Cal all year, and today was no different. On Tech’s next drive, what might have been a crucial stop on second and long turned into a facemask penalty that moved the Hokies into the red zone. Power back Marcellous Hawkins Jr. handled the next few plays and found the end zone, restoring Virginia Tech’s lead at 14-7. Cal then hit back-to-back 21-yard receptions to Jordan King and Ian Strong, setting up Townes McGough for a 35-yard field goal to end the half, 14-10. Midway through the third quarter, Cal converted a fake punt, with tight end Dorian Thomas running to the Tech 37. Change-up back Carson Perry-Smith acquitted himself well, helping advance the ball into the red zone, where the drive eventually stalled. Faced with 4th and goal from the Hokie 4-yard line, Cal sent out McGough for a field goal that left the Bears down 14-13 as the third quarter closed. A questionable targeting call against Cal, on what looked like a hard sack, extended a drive that would otherwise have been over and brought the Hokies to midfield. They capitalized, throwing their way into the red zone and facing 4th and 1 at the Cal 16, but the field goal attempt was once again wide left. Cal put together a successful drive on its next possession. The Bears briefly bogged down in the red zone but found the end zone on a tenuous-feeling 3rd and goal, with Perry-Smith making a leaping grab for the touchdown. Cal went for two and missed, but led 19-14 with just over four minutes remaining. Virginia Tech spent the next two minutes advancing to the Cal 11-yard line and began the final two minutes of regulation with a fresh set of downs. After 45 more seconds, Tech ran it in for a touchdown, but its own two-point attempt failed, putting the Hokies up 20-19 with 1:15 left. Cal’s final drive was aided by two costly Virginia Tech penalties, with RB Ashten Emory punching in a touchdown with 19 seconds remaining. The Bears again failed on the two-point try, but led 25-20. Virginia Tech made quick work of good field position, helped by more than 15 yards of Cal penalties, and reached first and goal at the Cal 7 with three seconds left. The final throw fell incomplete, handing Cal its first win over Virginia Tech since joining the ACC. Write For California is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Ugly game but we came up with the W. Why? In spite of some really stupid penalties and poor tackling after first contact on defense and missing a bunch of starters on both sides of the ball, our offensive play calling kept the VT defense off balance. What a difference a good play caller on offense makes. Somerville should go back to 12 year olds... Agree with Rugger...Play calling made all the difference and D did just enough. But more than that, I love the spirit of the team to hang in there no matter what. A winners mentality that starts from the top. In Tosh I trust. The three pillars emerged today and we got a win.

title: Leinster v Cardiff: Sam Prendergast stars in homecoming win that ends losing start to URC title defence - Planet Rugby
content:
Leinster fly-half Sam Prendergast in action against Cardiff. Leinster ended their two-game losing streak in the United Rugby Championship (URC) as they beat Cardiff 29-5 at the Laya Arena on Saturday. Scores from Hugo Keenan, Jimmy O’Brien (2), Jack Conan and Jamie Osborne helped the reigning champions to the bonus-point win on home soil. Sam Prendergast was the star though as his running game caught the eye and will be encouraging to Leo Cullen and Ireland head coach Andy Farrell. Meanwhile, Cardiff‘s only try of the game came through Mason Grady as they suffer their first defeat of the new URC season to end the round in sixth. A ruthless Leinster outfit had the try bonus point safely in their locker by half-time, thanks to those crossings from Keenan, O’Brien (2) and Conan. It took nine minutes to get on the board as the Ireland full-back’s perfectly weighted left-footed kick down the sideline sat up for him to gather and then dot down for an unconverted score. Keenan’s brilliance to make it 5-0 was rightly appreciated by the fans at their redeveloped venue. The Lions number 15 then turned provider on 17 minutes when a scrum move down the blindside saw him put O’Brien over for a close-range score. Prendergast was beginning to purr at this point and he ate up the ground with ball in hand before being scragged just metres away from the line. The resulting phase, however, saw the ball find Max Deegan who had Conan on his right running a smart line to make it a 15-0 Leinster lead. Cardiff did record a response on 24 minutes when quick thinking from Callum Sheedy off a penalty saw him pick out winger Grady who gathered well. Ulster v Munster: Five takeaways as hosts ‘flick a switch’ to overcome ‘men against boys’ start in heroic draw But normal service was resumed on 37 minutes as another superb break from Prendergast eventually saw him locate O’Brien out wide for his brace. Leading 22-5 at the half-time interval was a handy cushion but there were no further points during the opening 36 minutes of the second period. Indeed, Cardiff were growing in confidence and had the bulk of possession and territory around the hour mark, with Taine Basham prominent. However, the second-half drought would end with a Leinster try on 76 minutes when Osborne took a delayed Prendergast pass to add the gloss. The bonus-point win propels Leinster up the standings to 10th as the competition heads into a one-week break for the two European tournaments. Want more from Planet Rugby? title: The GAC Aion V Looks Odd But Is Incredible Value | Review - Carscoops
content:
GAC's Aion V represents exceptional value for money and is well worth considering If you walked up to someone on the street and asked them what a GAC Aion V was, most would give you a blank stare. Those brave enough to answer might think it’s a fancy new washing machine, while others may guess it’s the name of an advanced hot-water system. It’s actually an electric SUV, and it’s launched in several markets, eager to shake up the EV establishment. On paper, the Aion V seems almost too good to be true. This SUV promises space and comfort to match a Tesla Model Y, all while costing significantly less, having more impressive features, and being backed by one of China’s oldest and largest car manufacturers. However, as we’ve seen with many other new cars from China, the specification sheet only tells part of the story. Building a compelling electric SUV isn’t easy. Has GAC managed to create one with the Aion V? The answer is a resounding yes. Two versions of the Aion V are sold in Australia. The entry-level Aion V Premium kicks off the range, priced from AU$42,590 (US$29,700) before fees, while sitting at the top of the family is the Aion V Luxury, which we recently drove, priced at AU$44,590 (US$31,000) before fees. The Aion V is actually in its second generation, with this model first introduced in China in mid-2024. It’s underpinned by GAC’s AEP 3.0 platform, also used by the China-exclusive Toyota bZ3X. Several different battery packs are available depending on the region. These include a 62 kWh lithium-ion pack from CATL, a slightly larger 64.5-kWh LFP battery, a 75-kWH LFP, and a 90-kWh NMC battery. All versions sold in Australia come standard with the 75 kWh pack, directing power through a single front-mounted electric motor with 150 kW (201 hp) and 210 Nm (155 lb-ft)of torque. Although Chinese car brands have shown they can build cars at almost unthinkable price points, not all of them have figured out how to build a vehicle that’s nice to look at. As we experienced earlier this year with the Emzoom, M8 PHEV, and Aion UT, the Aion V isn’t exactly the most stylish SUV. It’s boxy, but not necessarily in a good way, and has a rather unusual stance on the road. Look past the odd design and peek inside the cabin, and you’ll understand where the Aion V starts to make a whole lot of sense. The interior of the Aion V doesn’t compute with an SUV that costs less than AU$45,000 (US$31,400), or roughly the same as a Toyota Corolla ZR, which is now almost a decade old. It feels so well put together, and so premium, that you could easily be fooled into thinking you were sitting in a vehicle costing upwards of AU$70,000 (US$48,900). Obviously, the 14.6-inch infotainment display is what immediately catches the eye. It’s crisp and snappy, housing all important vehicle controls, including the climate functions. We hate screens used to adjust temperature and fan speed as much as anyone, but at least the Aion V has a shortcut menu locked at the bottom of the screen with these controls, making them a little easier to access while on the move. The Aion V also comes standard with an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster and a two-spoke steering wheel. In Luxury guise, the EV also comes standard with genuine leather seats that feel exceptionally premium. Better yet, both front seats include superb massage functions that work absolutely brilliantly. Unlike so many massaging seats where you can only feel a tiny pulse in your back, the Aion V’s seats deliver a surprisingly realistic feel, as if tiny fists are being firmly pressed into your back. Usually, this is something you’ll only find in cars worth six figures. Review: China’s 2026 GAC Aion UT Is A Budget EV That Doesn’t Feel Cheap Perhaps the single biggest party piece of the Aion V’s cabin is the fridge. Housed between the front seats where you’d ordinarily find the center console, it’s 6.6 liters and proved hugely beneficial in hot weather, keeping my drink bottle cool. It’s not just a fridge either. The temperature can be adjusted to as low as 5 degrees Fahrenheit (-15 degrees Celsius), so it doubles as a freezer. What’s more, the temperature can be increased to up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius) should you want to keep drinks or food warm. All important interior surfaces feel very premium. These include the two-tone door panels with diamond stitching, the soft-touch dashboard, and the felt used for the wireless smartphone charger. The positives continue in the rear. While the Aion V’s 2,775-mm (109.2-inch) wheelbase isn’t huge, it feels certifiably palatial in the second row. There’s plenty of headroom and legroom for adults to sit comfortably in the back. The Luxury model even includes a fold-out table on the back of the front passenger seat. Add in a panoramic glass roof with a sliding cover – unlike a Tesla – and you get a cabin that feels beautifully executed. Unlike a Tesla Model Y, which even in its simplest form has a sporty edge to it, there’s nothing sporty about the Aion V. That’s not to say it isn’t a lovely place to spend time, as it is. Figures of 150 kW (201 hp) and 210 Nm (155 lb-ft) are par for the course for front-wheel drive EVs like this, matching figures like the Hyundai Elexio and Kia EV5, but down slightly on the Geely EX5 with its 160 kW (215 hp) and 320 Nm (236 lb-ft). Torque steer is kept to a minimum, although there is a hint of it if you pin the throttle in Sport mode. I spent most of the week with the Aion V driving around in Power Save mode as it’s the only mode that enabled one-pedal driving. This let me average just 14.8 kWh/100 km across more than 300 km (186 miles) of driving, meaning it is very possible to meet GAC’s WLTP-claimed driving range of 510 km (317 miles). The lack of one-pedal driving in Sport or Comfort modes is disappointing, as is the lack of paddle shifters to make on-the-fly adjustments to the regenerative braking. This isn’t a big deal, but it is something that prospective buyers should be aware of. Steering feel is good. Unlike some EVs, the Aion V’s steering isn’t so light that a strong gust of wind through an open window could turn the wheel. Instead, it’s nicely weighted, although it doesn’t do a good job of transmitting feedback from the road, so it can be a little difficult to determine what the front tires are up to. GAC has also done a good job of calibrating the suspension. The Aion UT I tested earlier this year rode more like a premium German sedan than a cheap, electric hatchback, and it’s much the same as the V. Owing to the SUV’s larger size, it is a little firmer than the UT, but it never crashes over potholes or speed bumps, and instead rides over them gracefully and quietly. Charging speeds are solid. GAC says the Aion V supports charging speeds of up to 180 kW, meaning the battery can be charged from 10-80 percent in roughly 24 minutes. While a base Tesla Model Y can charge at up to 250 kW, it costs roughly AU$13,000 (US$9,000) more than the Aion V. More direct rivals like the Geely EX5 and Hyundai Elexio have DC charging speeds capped at just 100 kW and 150 kW, respectively. It’s not all sunshine and rainbows, though. My biggest gripe with the Aion V is its safety systems, which are an all-too-common theme among Chinese EVs. First is the driver-monitoring system, which is as hyperactive as a kid that’s just eaten a whole bag of M&Ms. Glance away from the road for a split second and it’ll start complaining, triggering an annoying ring until you look back at the road. Similarly, the speed monitoring immediately alerts you even if you’re just momentarily 1 km/h over the speed limit. While these features are becoming more common, not just on cars from China but elsewhere in Asia, Europe, and the US, some brands have made it simple to disengage these alerts with conveniently placed shortcuts on the touchscreen. That’s not the case with the Aion V, as you have to dive into several menus to disable them every time you go for a drive. The GAC Aion V is very impressive, especially given the price and all of the equipment on offer. I have no doubt the exterior design will put off some in the market for an electric SUV, but if you can look past some of the odd styling, it’s a well-rounded proposition. For a vehicle costing less than AU$50,000 (US$34,900), the interior is the obvious highlight. It’s stylish, well-made, plush, and loaded with features. Combine a calming driving experience with great efficiency, and you get a mid-size electric SUV that’ll leave some legacy brands scratching their heads. title: Billy V’s HNN Sunrise surf and weather report for Oct. 10, 2026 - Hawaii News Now
content: HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - With the exception of an increase in showers Monday night on Hawaiʻi Island, conditions will be light to moderate trade winds returning. Showers will be mostly windward and mauka, primarily in the overnight hours. Daytime will feature relatively more drier trade winds across the pae ʻāina for the next week. Surf along south and west-facing shores will stay elevated but below advisory levels. It should ease through the weekend, then build again as a new swell arrives Saturday and peaks Sunday into Monday. North shore surf will remain small through the weekend, then increase to moderate levels when another swell arriving Monday and peaking Tuesday. East shore surf will stay small, with only minor changes expected because local winds are fairly weak. Small swells from Pacific storms may also pass through the islands this weekend. title: Ulster v Munster: Five takeaways as hosts 'flick a switch' to overcome 'men against boys' start in heroic draw - Planet Rugby
content: Munster centre Dan Kelly and Jacob Stockdale for Ulster. Following a 26-26 draw between Ulster and Munster in the United Rugby Championship, here’s our five takeaways from the game at Affidea Stadium. The game of two halves cliché is very apt for this Interpro match as Munster led 5-26 at the break before Ulster battled back to share the spoils. Crossings from Alex Kendellen (2), Marnus van der Merwe and Dan Kelly got Munster tails up, with JJ Hanrahan converting three of those tries. A 21-point advantage looked to be unassailable, especially with the one-sided nature of the half, but somehow Ulster turned things around, adding to Jacob Stockdale’s first-half score with another Stockdale crossing before Dave McCann and Stuart McCloskey grabbed seven-pointers. It felt like men against boys up front in the early knockings as the visitors turned the screw in the forward exchanges and it paid off in droves. Kendellen’s first and Van der Merwe’s try arrived inside 14 minutes as the scrum and maul bore fruit, leaving Ulster with a mountain to climb. It will no doubt be a worry for Richie Murphy going forward as opposing teams will see this as a weakness to squeeze, while for Munster it’s clear the signings of Springboks hooker Van der Merwe and former England tighthead prop Kieran Brookes have shored up their front-row. Stormers v Sharks: Five takeaways as Capetonians ‘turn the screw’ at scrum time while Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu ‘on a different planet’ The 29-year-old was outstanding this evening as he provided solidity in all aspects, offering real physicality and nailing his lineout throw-ins. Add in earning his side breakdown penalties and a try, and this was an outstanding showing from the former Cheetahs and Scarlets forward. He is already looking like one of the signings of the season after just three games, and keeping him fit will be key for Clayton McMillan’s side. “As bad an Ulster performance I have seen in a long time,” was the view of Premier Sports commentator Simon Zebo early in the second-half and it was hard to argue with the ex-Munster wing at that point. How they flicked a switch after that Zebo line as they looked like a different team. Want more from Planet Rugby? Conversely, the change from Munster was equally stark as they did not fire a shot in the second-half, being scoreless as they fumbled the win. “It will feel like a loss,” Zebo’s co-commentator Stephen Ferris said late on, summing up how they failed to finish what was a proverbial tap-in. Two tries for Stockdale was a rare positive for Ulster tonight, with his first a sublime finish before his second arrived from a great support line. Getting Stockdale back to his world-beating best form would be a massive fillip for both Ulster and Ireland this season, and judging from what he produced with the limited ball that came his way, the signs are good. title: Saracens v Bristol Bears: Five takeaways as Noah Caluori 'series two' gets underway in 'hearty stew' game that marks the 'duality of the PREM' - Planet Rugby
content: Noah Caluori (left) scoring v Bristol Bears in 2026 with an inset of Pat Lam Following Saracens’ 30-7 win over Bristol Bears at the StoneX, here are our five key takeaways from the PREM Rugby clash. Saracens responded to last weekend’s defeat to Sale Sharks in perfect fashion by thumping Bristol Bears on home soil. The first-half was pretty gritty and tight, with the Londoners only leading 11-0 at the break thanks to a Noah Caluori try and two penalties from Owen Farrell. A Harry Randall score threatened to bring Bristol back into the mix, but it proved mere consolation in the end as Saracens ran away with proceedings after that. Alex O’Driscoll, a penalty try and Jack Bracken made sure their dominance was converted into scoreboard points across the half, bagging them a bonus point in the process. Bristol looked to end on a high note with one final flurry with the clock in the red, but in a metaphor for the game as a whole, Saracens held them at bay and came away with the spoils. If you wanted to get a feel for the duality of the PREM, look no further than the two games today. The opener at Franklin’s Gardens was rock-and-roll rugby from both sides. It was fast and furious, too fast too furious for defensive coaches maybe, but it ended with 18 tries and some showreel stuff at that. Basketball-like, to use a common comparison. Northampton Saints v Bath: Winners and losers as forgotten England man ‘right on the money’ while Test bolters ‘stand tall’ But this game in North London was not that. It wasn’t even close. Only one try was scored in the entirety of the first-half, and that came inside the opening five minutes, while only two more were added to that tally after the break. To put it into comparison, Ollie Sleightholme and Arthur Green scored the same number of tries as any of the 46 players involved in this game. It was gripping, intriguing and genuinely entertaining. It was rugby at its tactical, methodical best. It was like a proper game of chess. The lack of points wasn’t through a lack of intent, either, but rather defensive solidity. Saracens posted just 20 missed tackles across the 80 minutes, with the likes of Phil Brantingham, Olamide Sodeke, Maro Itoje and George Martin getting stuck into proceedings on that front. Saracens did eventually cut loose, but the tone was set by their grit early on. The game in the East Midlands felt like a luxurious, rich chocolate cake, one you only have on rare occasions, but this was an autumnal bowl of hearty stew. It was warming for the soul. Four minutes and one touch. That’s how long it took Caluori series two to get properly underway, and it only got better from there. The winger, who burst onto the scene last year for both club and country, was a real fiend across the 80 minutes, consistently having big impacts on the game. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Every time he touched the ball in attack, things seemed to happen. His try came after being given just a glimmer of space and was finished while under pressure, and he made a similarly impressive half-break in the second-half to create the chance for O’Driscoll’s try. He was also heavily involved in the build-up for Bracken’s score too, floating off his wing and adding a key link. His stats sheet was a reflection of his efforts, too, posting 102 metres from his eight carries alongside three defenders beaten and one full linebreak across a busy shift. This felt like a big season for the youngster, with people wondering if second season syndrome would kick in; but on this showing, it seems he is no flash in the pan. Caluori series two is up and running, and the first episode has got rave reviews. Bristol Bears were flying this time last week. They’d just beaten Northampton Saints, which came a week on from them doing a job on Sale Sharks. They were second in the PREM table, and boasted maximum points. But this defeat has brought them crashing back to Earth. It’s an early season reality check. Saracens certainly deserve the bulk of the plaudits for the manner of their victory, as they suffocated the Bears. But Bristol played a part in it too. Pat Lam’s side posted 51% territory in the first-half, but barely fired a shot with that. Their one big chance came late in the half, with Louis Rees-Zammit looking to send Sam Worsley waltzing in for an easy score, only for J. Bracken to produce a piece of defensive magic to dive and steal the ball mid-air. To make matters worse, they were playing with an advantage, and from the subsequent lineout they were pinged and saw the chance go begging. Harry Randall’s score got them back into the game, but it was again the only shot they fired in the second-half as Saracens again put their foot on the throat. The yellow card also didn’t help things, and it made the scoreline quite ugly. Leicester v Gloucester: Five takeaways as ‘up since 3am’ Wales star gives Tigers’ season ‘a right royal kick-start’ in front of Duke of Sussex Bristol’s wait for a win at the StoneX continues, and it should act as a reality check for the Bears after a blistering start to the season. They will come back stronger, though. Ahaha, wine joke. Get it? Nobody’s made them this week! But in all seriousness, it seems there is a real identity forming with Saracens now, when you look at this game and compare it to their opening two games. It was much more like their win over Leicester Tigers than the Sale Sharks game, which is pleasing for the coaching staff. They just look hungry in every department. The set-piece fired brilliantly; they showed further ambition in attack and a desire to go wide but also knew they had to earn it. In saying that, they were again just hungry to break through the gainline in the tight, using their key battering rams to good effect in those close exchanges. The combination of Owen Farrell and Caluori also worked wonders in the aerial game. Like any good wine, Saracens are maturing well into the new season. You think they’ll only continue to get better from here. Lucky to avoid red card for his reactionary shove on Rodrigo Bentancur? 6 Kobbie Mainoo: Caught in possession on too many occasions, even if the passes he was receiving inside his own half were ill-advised. title: All Blacks v Wallabies prediction: 'Battered' New Zealand to lose Eden Park record in Bledisloe Cup opener - Planet Rugby
content:
Cam Roigard and Ryan Lonergan face off at Eden Park on Saturday. A battered New Zealand side without its captain and both first-choice fly-halves meets Les Kiss’ unbeaten Wallabies, fresh from beating the world champions, in Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup opener at Eden Park. There are older rivalries in the game, but not many, and few that have been played as often or as hard as this one. New Zealand and Australia first met in a Test in 1903, the Bledisloe Cup has been fought over since the early 1930s, and for the last two decades the story has been told almost entirely in black: the All Blacks have held the Cup since 2003, they’ve won their last 11 Tests against the Wallabies, and Australia haven’t won at Eden Park since 1986. On paper, then, it says New Zealand. The present is more complicated, because the All Blacks come into this game battered and bruised by a heavy-format, four-Test series against the Springboks that started with a 33-16 win at Ellis Park and then turned into three straight defeats, the last of them 43-28 in Baltimore. The bill has arrived in the shape of a casualty list that would test any squad. Ardie Savea dislocated his shoulder in Soweto and is very unlikely to play again this year, Luke Jacobson has had elbow surgery, Ruben Love’s ankle has finished his 2026, and Richie Mo’unga tore a calf in training on Tuesday. Add Caleb Clarke, Billy Proctor, Anton Lienert-Brown and Fehi Fineanganofo and you’ve a side missing its captain, both its first-choice fly-halves and two of its three best loose forwards; Damian McKenzie moves to fly-half, Beauden Barrett comes in at full-back and Codie Taylor leads the side. Australia, by contrast, are flying. Kiss hasn’t lost since taking over from Joe Schmidt: two wins over Japan, a win and a draw in Argentina that gave the Wallabies their first ever series win there, and then the 42-38 victory over the Springboks in Perth, a game they had led by 25 points and finished with 11 men. Hunter Paisami’s suspension is the only forced change, with Len Ikitau moving to 12 and Isaac Henry starting at 13, and it makes for two very exciting teams and the most genuine sense in years that the Bledisloe is up for grabs. The Wallabies have to win the two-Test series outright to take the Cup back, and the second Test is in Sydney a week on Saturday. Two things will shape this Test: what happens to the ball when it goes up, and how rarely it goes to ground. Start with the air, because both coaches have picked their sides with it in mind. Kiss has kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing alongside Max Jorgensen and Tom Wright because the aerial contest decided Perth, where a Ryan Lonergan box kick left Aphelele Fassi one-on-one with Suaalii and led to Ikitau’s second try. New Zealand have good reason to be wary, because across the four Tests against South Africa they secured only 30 per cent of contestable kicks, and Leroy Carter, the smallest man in their back three, can expect a fair amount of traffic. It will be a low-ruck game, and deliberately so. Every breakdown is another opportunity to lose possession, concede a penalty or allow the defence to reset, and with Fraser McReight hunting over the ball, New Zealand have every reason to keep those contests to a minimum. McReight is one of the most destructive breakdown operators in Test rugby, and the last thing the All Blacks want is to feed him a succession of predictable carries into a settled line, so both sides will favour the aerial contest and the chance to attack before the defence resets rather than carry repeatedly into an organised one. It’s a calculated risk, because every loose contestable kick also gives McReight and his fellow chasers the chance to turn defence into attack, and in a match with fewer breakdowns, a single turnover in the right part of the field could be decisive. Barrett brothers set for stunning post-World Cup switch as PREM Rugby pair enter tug of war for All Blacks greats Australia will also fancy their chances against a New Zealand defence that hasn’t been watertight. The All Blacks shipped six tries and 43 points in Baltimore, and on Saturday they will defend with a fly-half who has spent most of the year at full-back, a reshaped midfield and a back-row that has barely played together. Ikitau and Henry are big, direct runners who will go looking for McKenzie’s channel, and if the Wallabies can get Carter defending one-on-one on the left edge, he will have a long evening. Then there’s the maul, a key battle because both sides love a rumble. The Springboks showed both these teams how it works: Malcolm Marx scored off the drive in Soweto and again in Baltimore, and Johan Grobbelaar went over from one in Perth. Australia are very good at defending the drive, but Grobbelaar’s try was a reminder that one lapse is all it takes, and with Taylor throwing to Scott Barrett and Josh Lord, New Zealand will test that defence every time they get a penalty in the Wallaby half. That’s why discipline matters so much: the All Blacks conceded 43 penalties across the four Tests against the Springboks to South Africa’s 35 and lost eight lineouts on their own throw to South Africa’s two, and whichever side wins those columns on Saturday will have the platform to maul. And then there are the benches, and above all the replacement front-rows. Can Australia’s match New Zealand’s? It’s a big challenge. The All Blacks can bring on Asafo Aumua’s carrying, George Bower and Pasilio Tosi, all seasoned Test men, whereas Australia’s trio of Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, the former All Black facing his old side for the first time, and the 22-year-old Massimo De Lutiis is light on Test miles. Taniela Tupou is unavailable because he plays overseas and the release regulation isn’t in force for this October window. New Zealand will expect to turn the screw in the last quarter, exactly when the Springboks ran in 21 points in Perth. Kiss does have Nick Champion de Crespigny among his loose-forward cover, and if the Wallabies find themselves in trouble late on, a cool head in a crisis runs in the family: his uncle Richard was the Qantas captain who landed the stricken A380, QF32, at Singapore in 2010 with an engine blown apart and a badly damaged wing. Rennie’s respect for the Wallabies is genuine. After Perth he said Australia had been excellent, that he wasn’t surprised, and that it was “a good message for our boys” about the quality of the side coming to Eden Park. Scott Barrett shrugged off Rennie’s description of him as a “reluctant captain”, and said he was hugely excited to be back. On what’s coming, he was in no doubt: “We’re fully on alert.” Wallabies: The ‘Bermuda Triangle’ challenge facing ‘big body’ Joseph Suaalii on the Eden Park wing Kiss called Henry’s selection a fairly simple decision in the end, describing him as a team-first player who works hard on his craft and “just happens to be bloody talented too”. On his back three, he simply said he wanted to persist with the combination for another week. If there is one name the Wallabies should be worrying about on the All Blacks bench, it’s Anton Segner, the German-born Blues flanker who only made his Test debut this year and is an outstanding young openside. His game is built on exactly what matters in a low-ruck Test: low, hard tackling that stops carriers behind the gain line, strong hands over the ball and real footwork when he has it. When he comes on against a tiring Wallaby back-row he will be hunting the turnover that swings a tight game. With Jacobson out until next season, this is his chance to make the No.7 jersey his own. It’s been a strange year for Scott Barrett, or Scooter as everyone in New Zealand rugby knows him. A sabbatical, a back injury and the loss of the captaincy meant that when he turned out for Taranaki last month it was his first game in 10 months, but he is 89 Tests in and he is exactly what this pack has been missing: a lineout caller who wins his own ball, a big body behind Fletcher Newell at scrum time and a forward who relishes the dirty work. Harry Wilson against Wallace Sititi is another lovely contest. Wilson is the Wallaby captain and the heartbeat of their carrying game, a big, honest runner who scored in Perth, whilst Sititi is the more explosive athlete, with footwork and offloads that let him beat the first man rather than run through him. If the young All Black wins the collisions, Australia’s go-forward dries up quickly. The full-backs are a terrific contest. Wright has been one of Australia’s most consistent performers this season, dangerous on the counter and secure under the high ball, whilst Barrett, a 145-Test veteran, still has the range and the vision to turn a loose kick into a try from deep. Up front, the monster battle is Angus Bell against Newell, loosehead against tighthead. Bell is the most dynamic loosehead Australia have produced in years, a prop who carries like a back-rower and has become a far more reliable scrummager, whilst Newell is a superb tighthead whose job is to hold him up and drive through him. Cam Roigard against Lonergan is the best contest on the field, and it’s a proper clash of styles. Lonergan was absolutely brilliant against South Africa, scoring 17 points, kicking everything off the tee until a final conversion from out wide and putting on a box-kicking display so accurate that it gave the Wallabies the control they had lacked from their half-backs for years. Harry Wilson explains the ‘really good pictures’ Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry painted for the Wallabies Roigard is a different animal: quicker, more dangerous around the fringes and better at punishing a defence that isn’t set, but the only flaw in his rounded game is he is just a smidgen away in terms of the speed of base to foot kicking game that Lonergan possesses. The Wallabies will want to slow New Zealand’s ruck ball, because Roigard on quick ball against a retreating defence is the All Blacks’ best weapon, whilst New Zealand will want a fast chase onto Lonergan’s box kicks to make him hurry. Whichever nine controls the tempo will go a long way to deciding the Test. This writer tipped South Africa by 15 before Perth when every instinct (and indeed, the first draft) said Australia, and he is not making the same mistake twice. This is a coaching call, not a sentimental one. In Perth the Springbok blitz buried Ben Donaldson early, targeting the first receiver and slowing the Wallaby ball, and within the half, not at the break, Kiss’ side changed the picture: McReight, Wilson, Rob Valetini and Paisami took on first-receiver duties, Donaldson moved to second receiver, and suddenly the press was committing to the wrong threats. That’s a side that can alter the geometry of a Test in real time, and it’s exactly the wrong opponent for a New Zealand defence with McKenzie back at 10, a reshaped midfield and a back-row that has barely played together. When New Zealand change the defensive picture, this Wallaby side has shown it can find answers, and with McReight over the ball and Lonergan in control, Australia have the tools to win on their own terms, so long as they can overcome the emotional fortress that’s Eden Park. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. New Zealand will have their moments. Scott Barrett gives them an edge at the set-piece, their bench front-row is the stronger and Eden Park will roar them on, so Australia will need their bench to hold firm and keep their discipline in the last 20 minutes in a way they didn’t in Perth. But they are the better-organised side, they are coached by a man who solves problems while the match is happening, and they are playing a New Zealand team still finding out who it is. Australia to win 32-27 and end the Eden Park run, leaving the Wallabies one win in Sydney on October 17 away from their first Bledisloe Cup since 2002. title: Stormers v Sharks: Five takeaways as Capetonians 'turn the screw' at scrum time while Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu 'on a different planet' - Planet Rugby
content: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu impressed for the Stormers. Following a 39-22 victory for the Stormers over the Sharks in Cape Town, here’s our player ratings from the United Rugby Championship clash. The Sharks had their two-game winning streak ended on Saturday as they went down to an impressive Stormers side in this South African derby. Seabelo Senatla, Hacjivah Dayimani (2), Leolin Zas, Andre-Hugo Venter and JJ Kotze crossed for the hosts in a thoroughly deserved triumph. Manu Tshituka, Matt Romao and Phepsi Buthelezi got the Sharks’ tries as they were second best up front, suffering a first URC loss of the season. Indeed, the Capetonians turned the screw at the scrum today (more on that below) and that helped lay the platform for their backline to profit. It was a frustrating afternoon for Sharks props Ox Nche and Thomas du Toit, with the latter especially being pinged several times at the scrum. Up against Wilco Louw and Ntuthuko Mchunu respectively, the Sharks duo coughed up four penalties in the first-half at the scrum, and things didn’t get much better in the second as an early pushover try from the set-piece summed up the Stormers’ success in this facet of play. Of course, dominance in this area shouldn’t be attributed to any one thing or player, with credit therefore going to all of the Stormers’ forwards. Bulls player ratings: ‘Brutal’ Cameron Hanekom ‘bullies his opponents’ while Willie le Roux ‘unpicks’ the visitors Denied a hat-trick due to a Damian Willemse knock-on, but a treble would have been just rewards for Dayimani after a fine day at the office. He dovetailed nicely with the double openside threat of Siya Kolisi and Paul de Villiers today and with a tight five that was flexing all afternoon, Dayimani was able to capitalise in the wide open spaces. A brace was his return on a day the Stormers pack made a real statement. It might not have been a faultless showing off the kicking tee, but in all other areas, the Springboks fly-half was on a different planet today. The extra second a player has in possession is a sign of their quality and Feinberg-Mngomezulu appeared to have two today; such was his impact on the field. Playing with a smile on his face, he unlocked holes for others and himself, kicked brilliantly territorially and was a running threat to boot. This performance is an encouraging sign, not just for the Stormers but also the Boks in November’s Tests. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The Springboks veteran’s game lasted just 35 minutes as he eventually departed, this after struggling with what appeared to be a knee problem. The Sharks medical staff did attempt to relieve the pain by strapping the lock up, but their efforts proved unsuccessful as he was replaced. Rassie Erasmus will no doubt be straight on the phone to the second-row to ascertain the severity of the injury with the hope his exit was precautionary rather than anything more serious. JP Pietersen will also be interested as matches at Lyon, Cardiff and Munster await in October. title: Northampton Saints v Bath: 5 takeaways as England international acts as the 'sole of the Shoe Army' - Planet Rugby
content: Ollie Sleightholme (right) was a key performer in Northampton Saints' win over Bath Following Northampton Saints’ 71-48 win over Bath at Franklin’s Gardens, here are our five key takeaways from the PREM Rugby clash. Anyone tuning in late at DPD Franklin’s Gardens could be forgiven for thinking they’d stumbled on a cricket score, and by the end Saints were 71 for 7 with Bath all out for 48. April’s meeting finished 41-38, which at the time looked like a shootout, but this one went considerably further, with 18 tries shared between the sides and a combined 119 points, the second-highest in the league’s history behind the 127 Saints and Bristol put up at the same ground in May. The man in the middle was Matthew Carley, the most exacting referee in the league and normally the official least likely to let a game run away from everybody. Seeing him preside over this was like watching a Swiss train pull in twenty minutes late with the driver waving cheerfully from the cab. Carley let it flow because both sides wanted to play, and neither defence could stop the other one doing so. Strangest of all, the most box-office player in English rugby barely featured in the highlights. Henry Pollock made 15 tackles, fourth on the pitch, but didn’t make the top ten for carries, and his most memorable contribution was standing in at scrum-half for a lineout move. Callum Chick did the heavy carrying instead, 13 of them, whilst packing down on the flank and letting Pollock lean in at the base of the scrum on Saints ball. Ollie Sleightholme finished with a hat-trick, 101 running metres, nine defenders beaten and two clean breaks, top of all three lists, and every one of his tries came by a different route. The first, on 17 minutes, came from a set play built to exploit a narrow defence: Saints kicked a penalty to the corner, went long to the back of the lineout with Alex Mitchell in the line and Pollock at nine, ran three men short into the midfield, brought James Pater into the line and let the full-back fire a 35-metre pass to the left wing. Bath had packed in so tightly that there was nobody out there. Leicester v Gloucester: Five takeaways as ‘up since 3am’ Wales star gives Tigers’ season ‘a right royal kick-start’ in front of Duke of Sussex The second came on the counter, Tommy Freeman breaking out from a Bath attack on the Saints 22 and the ball going left through the hands, and the third was off a scrum, Sleightholme coming in at second receiver and going through untouched. The Shoe Army made itself heard each time, and they’ve every reason to, because their winger is in the form of his life. Both sets of half-backs were excellent, but they went about it in completely different ways, and each man’s method was a fair picture of how his side attacked. Finn Russell stood absurdly flat, attacking the line himself and passing in front of the man, and Bath followed him: smash it up, recycle fast and go again. His offload put Santi Carreras over on eight minutes, his quick tap penalty set up Charlie Griffin’s try, and his pass over the top for Carreras’s second, after a Tom Carr-Smith 50:22, was as good as anything all afternoon. Fin Smith worked more through the loop, coming round and distributing, and Saints were subtler with it, using big carries to commit defenders before shifting the point of attack and sending runners through the seam. He scored the opening try himself after JJ van der Mescht took three Bath defenders to stop him and the fold defence stepped in to cover, which left the gap on the outside. Smith threw 22 passes and kicked from hand only once in the first half; Russell kicked twice. Neither 10 had any interest in kicking the ball away, which goes some way to explaining the scoreline. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. His partner Mitchell also seems to have given England something to think about. With the game at 38-41 and swinging back and forth, it needed a moment of individual brilliance, and he provided it in the 56th minute. From a Saints scrum 38 metres out, he broke down the open side, where Bath had a reshuffled back row following Miles Reid’s early departure and Russell defending wide, grubbered through, regathered and scored on his own. It was the try that put Saints in front for good, and it came straight off a set piece that was flawless by half-time, 100 per cent at scrum and lineout against Bath’s 75 and 67. Mitchell was at the heart of almost everything Saints did well, sharp around the fringes and quick to punish any loose defender, and England’s coaches will have liked what they saw. Bath deserve real credit, because for long spells they played the smarter rugby. They invited Saints to kick, which Saints mostly declined to do, and played with cheek and impudence, none more so than Carreras, who trapped a contestable with his foot and flicked it up into his hands, finished with two tries and made 49 metres. Arthur Green carried 16 times, more than anyone on the pitch, and scored twice. PREM Rugby, round three: Predictions, teams, kick-off times, how to watch and referee appointments Their best spell came with Josh Bayliss in the sin bin for not rolling away. Freeman scored from the resulting penalty to put Saints 19-14 up, but Bath then scored 12 points with 14 men, Archie Griffin crashing over off a basketball pass from Carr-Smith and Kepu Tuipulotu breaking straight from the restart to put Green away. Tuipulotu finished with two turnovers, the most in the game. When Green scored again immediately after half-time, Bath were 36-26 up. Then, four minutes later, Carreras fumbled a routine pass with an overlap outside him and Pater picked up and ran 40 metres, a 14-point swing that turned the afternoon. Both coaches will spend the coming week on the same two subjects. By half-time Saints’ tackle success stood at 78% and Bath’s at 75, with 26 missed tackles between them, and it didn’t improve after the break. Curtis Langdon led the way with 17 tackles and Alex Coles and Cleopas Kundiona made 16 each, so plenty of people were trying, but the system in front of them kept springing leaks. Saints’ restarts were a particular problem, mishandled or poorly chased on almost every occasion, and Bath scored directly from two of them, Tuipulotu’s break on 33 minutes and Green’s second straight after half-time, when Saints simply didn’t guard the blindside. Bath’s own discipline failed them late on, Ollie Lawrence yellow-carded on 62 minutes for killing a ruck as Saints went fast and deep from their own 22, and Sleightholme completed his hat-trick within a minute. Coles, who also scored and made four defenders beaten, and Freeman, with his second try on 75 minutes, took Saints to 71 points and the win. title: Probable Formation: Como v Roma - Chiesa Di Totti
content: No Svilar, no Cristante - there’ll be a slightly different look to Roma as they return from a three-week break. After a three-week break, Roma pick things back up with a trip to face Como on matchday six of the Serie A season. Roma built some serious momentum in the first block of fixtures this season, but now will be forced to make at least a couple of tweaks to the formula against Como - and they’re significant ones. Add Chiesa Di Totti as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. Most concerningly of all, Mile Svilar has been ruled out for a few weeks with a toe injury, which will bring an end to his 95-game starting streak in Serie A. Pierluigi Gollini will take his place for what will be his league debut in Roma colors, nearly two years after joining. “Gollini is a goalkeeper who, in his career, has perhaps only played consistently with me,” Gian Piero Gasperini said at his press conference of his former Atalanta keeper. “I’ve reunited with him here at Roma after a bit of a stint with a few other teams. He’s definitely an excellent second goalkeeper. Now he has the opportunity to play consistently. “When I had him at Atalanta, he even got called up to the national team, playing as third goalkeeper for a long time, at least for a couple of years. So he definitely has the ability and value. He’s always trained well in recent months and must have everyone’s trust, because we’re not fielding a goalkeeper who’s never played. He’s a guy who will now have the chance to show consistency.” In addition, an injury to captain Bryan Cristante has been one of the main Roma talking points from the extended international break. Until now, only Svilar has amassed more minutes of gametime for Roma this season than their number four. Love him or hate him, losing a player that Gasperini has been so content to build around is a blow for a Roma side looking to pick up from where they left off. But as one of the squad’s leaders takes a backseat, another should return to contention. Lorenzo Pellegrini is yet to play this season after signing his contract extension in the summer, with injury keeping him on the sidelines. But not for much longer. There are even some indications that Pellegrini could slot straight into the starting lineup against Como, leading the team out as captain on what would be his 350th appearance. But it wouldn’t be in Cristante’s place on the pitch; instead, he’d be playing on the left side of the attacking midfield pair behind the striker. It’s the role that Roma drew most scrutiny for failing to reinforce in the summer. So far, they have had to adapt this season by switching up the responsibilities of Matías Soulé or Paulo Dybala, while also bedding in Rodrigo Mora. Mora was the busiest Roma player during the international break while on duty with Portugal’s under-21s - and he made the most of it with an overhead kick goal - but understandably isn’t yet a nailed-on starter for his new club. And with Dybala and Soulé both more effective from the right - the former is the more likely starter for this assignment, for what it’s worth, due to the latter travelling back from Argentina this week with Santiago Castro and Leonardo Balerdi - it makes sense for Gasperini to lean back on the experience of Pellegrini on the left if he is up to speed. “Before the break, I’d been on the bench twice, but I’d just come back and wasn’t ready yet,” Pellegrini said this week, at an event for the Premio Giuseppe Colalucci. “This break came at the perfect time, because I had the chance to train, push hard, and even test things out. I’m really happy and super pumped for this restart.” As for the Cristante replacement, experience could be the order of the day again, with Maarten de Roon seemingly in pole position over Niccolò Pisilli to partner Manu Koné. De Roon has only made appearances off the bench since reuniting with Gasperini at Roma, but had no national team commitments during the break and should have been able to get more in tune with his new surroundings at club level. Roma’s other new absentee is Konstantinos Koulierakis, who should be able to return to the fold next week. It isn’t a major issue for Gasperini, who is yet to deploy the Greek international as a starter and has Evan Ndicka available again at the back after he missed the Inter game before the international break. Any concerns about Donyell Malen’s availability have also been washed away, with Roma ready to rely on their talisman as usual. ROMA (3-4-2-1): Gollini; Mancini, Ndicka, Hermoso; Molina, De Roon, Koné, Wesley; Dybala, Pellegrini; Malen. As if the Como match wasn’t tough enough already, Roma must conquer I Lariani without Mile Svilar in goal. After scoring six goals in five matches, Malen was an easy choice for Player of the Month. Rodrigo Mora is still adapting to Serie A, but his role in Gasperini’s attack already reveals his enormous potential. Balerdi came in as a Plan D after several other moves fell through. You can’t tell from his play in a Roma kit. Marten de Roon has played sparingly, but his role under Gasperini is already clear: stabilize matches and protect leads. title: The V-Twin Engine That Gives Riders Big Power Without Big Ownership Costs - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Big displacement has always meant big bills. It’s an old rule of thumb in motorcycling that most riders absorb without ever being told. After all, a huge engine needs a huge purchase price, a huge service invoice, and a shelf of expensive parts waiting for their turn to fail. Therefore, general wisdom says that if you want a cruiser that whisks you along the road with real authority, you should be ready to pay for the privilege. It's a reasonable assumption that exists because it is the reality for plenty of bikes. However, a well-engineered V-Twin, built by a company that built durability above all else, can deliver serious muscle without turning ownership into a second job. The charm of a big V-Twin is obvious. They make torque you can feel in your chest, they sound like authority on the road, and they give a cruiser a presence that smaller engines can't fake. However, premium cruisers tend to arrive with premium price tags before you've ridden a single mile. Complex engines can mean long service visits and expensive labor. Modern cruisers come with sensors, modules, and displays that are wonderful when they work and painful when they don't. Specialized parts also cost more, and a lot of routine maintenance ends up being something only the dealer is able to handle. Then there are the tires, brakes, and consumables sized for a big V-Twin cruiser. Everything is a little bigger, a little stronger, and a little more expensive than it would be on a smaller bike. Most riders accept this as the cost of entry. If you want big power, you budget for big upkeep and hope for the best. The interesting question is whether that bargain is really unavoidable. Suzuki's Boulevard M109R is one of the more convincing arguments that it isn't. It arrived in 2006 as the company's flagship power cruiser, and it was aimed at riders who wanted V-Twin muscle and were happy to get it from a Japanese manufacturer known for building things that last. The formula is straightforward: a large liquid-cooled engine, shaft drive, and a conventional cruiser layout with no unnecessary drama. The M109R didn't take its engine from the usual cruiser playbook. Suzuki borrowed fuel-injection technology from its GSX-R sportbikes, and the design shows it. The engine uses liquid cooling, four valves per cylinder, and two spark plugs on each cylinder, all managed by a modern engine computer. The cylinders are lined with Suzuki's own SCEM coating, which helps shed heat and lets the pistons run with tight clearances. The internals are just as ambitious. The forged aluminum-alloy pistons are among the largest ever fitted to a production motorcycle, at 112 mm across. It's sport bike thinking applied to a cruiser, and it's a big part of why the engine feels so sturdy. An engine that's strong and well cooled from the start is an engine that can live a long, unfussy life. You don't need constant attention when the hardware is built for the work. The M109R runs a 1,783 cc, V-Twin with a 112.0 x 90.5 mm bore and stroke and a 10.5:1 compression ratio. Suzuki's claimed output is 128 horsepower, with 118 lb-ft of torque arriving at just 3,200 rpm. These numbers put the M109R in serious company. Plenty of cruisers make lots of torque, but few pair it with triple-digit horsepower, and the combination is what gives the bike its personality. You get the low-rpm shove that cruiser riders love, plus a strong pull as the revs build. It’s big too. The Suzuki Boulevard M109R weighs 764 pounds wet and features a 5.2-gallon fuel tank, and the wheelbase is a long 67.3 inches. A seat height of just 27.8 inches helps balance that, keeping the bike approachable at a standstill and putting your feet flat on the ground when it matters most. The power reaches the road through a five-speed gearbox and a shaft final drive. It's a simple, sturdy layout, and it suits an engine that makes most of its muscle low in the rev range. You rarely need to work the gearbox hard, because a twist of the throttle in almost any gear gets the bike moving with authority. Suzuki also made sure the hardware around the engine could handle the output. Later models get radially mounted twin front discs, ABS, and LED lighting, and the rear end wears a 240/40 R18 tire to put all that torque on the ground. The result is a cruiser that feels effortless. It isn't trying to be a sportbike, and it doesn't need to. It just pulls, smoothly and steadily, in a way that makes a long stretch of highway feel like a short one. Routine service is simple. Maintenance charts commonly list oil and filter changes at about 3,500 miles or once a year, with plugs and air filter checked at the same time. Shaft drive removes the chain from the equation entirely, so there's no cleaning, lubing, or adjusting, and the final drive just needs its oil changed at longer intervals. The engine's most significant scheduled job is the valve clearance check, which Suzuki's service information puts at roughly every 14,500 miles. That's a real task, and it's not free. Some rivals use hydraulic valve systems that skip this step entirely. But it's an infrequent job, the interval is long, and a few hundred dollars every few years is hardly a budget-breaker for a bike this size. Tires are the honest exception. Those wide 130/70 R18 and 240/40 R18 tires are expensive, and replacing a set can often cost beyond $500. They also tend to wear out faster if you have a heavy throttle hand. The purchase price is where the M109R really stands out. The 2025 model has an MSRP of $15,799, which is not little money but is a long way from the price of a fully-loaded flagship touring cruiser. The cruiser’s reliability also means that a lot of buyers are shopping the used market for the M109R, and buyers' guides have listed typical asking prices in the range of roughly $9,500 to $14,000, depending on year, mileage, and condition. No motorcycle with 1,783 cc of displacement is going to be free to own, and the M109R doesn't pretend otherwise. It's heavy, its tires cost real money, and its valves need attention on a schedule. Anyone telling you a bike like this costs nothing to run is selling something. But the details add up to a convincing case. The engine is well-built, with sport bike-derived engineering underneath. The service schedule is long and easy to follow. Shaft drive takes away one of the most annoying chores in motorcycling. And Suzuki's reputation for durability counts for something when you're buying a machine this big and this powerful. Add it up and the pattern-breaking idea holds. The M109R gives riders the muscle, the sound, and the presence of a big V-Twin, and it does so without the expensive electronics and dealer-only service that usually come with that territory. For the right buyer, that's a rare combination. Big power doesn't have to mean big bills. Sometimes it just means finding the engine that was engineered to make the trade-off unnecessary. title: Aston Villa v Brentford - Match Preview, kick-off time & more - Brentford FC
content:
Analysis, team news, match officials and more. Here's everything you need to know ahead of Brentford's Premier League game against Aston Villa at Villa Park on Saturday afternoon (3pm kick-off BST) Analysis, team news, match officials and more - here's everything you need to know ahead of the game. Brentford return to action after an extended international break looking to harness the momentum built by their best-ever start to a Premier League season. The Bees signed off in style three weeks ago, sweeping Chelsea aside 3-0 at Gtech Community Stadium to move fourth in the table and extend their unbeaten start to seven games across all competitions. Keith Andrews' side have spent just three minutes and 10 seconds behind in the Premier League this term, while their intensity without the ball has been equally striking: Brentford rank second in the division for sprints, with September Player of the Month nominee Kevin Schade and Igor Thiago both among the competition's five most prolific sprinters. The Bees also appear to have honed one of their traditional strengths. Brentford lead the league for set-piece xG and xG per corner, with Jaidon Anthony's opener against Chelsea the latest evidence of their threat from dead-ball situations. At the other end of the pitch, Brentford have posted some encouraging defensive numbers. Only Everton and Leeds (three goals apiece) have conceded fewer than the Bees (four) over the first five games of the season, with Vitaly Janelt and Kristoffer Ajer among their standout performers. Janelt has made more interceptions (16) than any other Premier League player this term, while Ajer currently ranks fourth in the division for both clearances and aerial duels won. Both return from productive international breaks on a personal level: Janelt made his senior Germany debut in a 2-0 win over Serbia, while Ajer scored a thunderous volley in Norway's 2-1 defeat to Portugal last weekend. Ajer has been colossal at the back alongside either Jannik Schuster or Nathan Collins, and the Bees' collective strength in the air may be significant on Saturday. Brentford have won more aerial duels per game (21.6) than any team in the Premier League this season, while Saturday's opponents Villa have won fewer (9) than any other side. After winning the Europa League last season, Villa are a team in transition. With the likes of Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Emiliano Martínez all departing Villa Park in the summer, the Midlanders have endured a slow start and currently rank bottom of the top flight for both shots (9.6) and shots on target (2.4) per game. However, there were signs that Villa's new-look squad was starting to click in their 3-2 victory over Spurs. Japan international Zion Suzuki has made a positive impact between the sticks for the Villans, the 24-year-old former Parma keeper making some outstanding saves in the win at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson also scored their first Premier League goals in Villa colours in north London, with the lively forward duo offering plenty of encouragement that they can play important roles for Emery this season. In addition to beating the Midlands club on penalties in the Carabao Cup, Brentford completed a league double over Villa last season. Intriguingly, the Bees recorded their two lowest possession shares of the entire 2025/26 league campaign in those 1-0 victories (24 per cent at home and 28 per cent away), showcasing their resilience and ability to hurt teams without much of the ball. With Emery's side no doubt eager to avenge three defeats last term, it will be fascinating to see whether Andrews takes a similar approach at Villa Park or looks to impose the high-energy, front-footed football that has served Brentford so well this season. For the second time in three seasons, Aston Villa finished fourth last term as they continued to reestablish themselves as one of the Premier League’s heavy hitters. Between 28 September and 27 December, Unai Emery’s side won 12 of their 13 league games and, for long periods, looked capable of finishing in the top three for only the second time in their history. Results were far too inconsistent throughout the second half of 2025/26 for that - they won six of the last 18, for context. But Champions League qualification was secured again. Not that they needed their league position to secure it, mind you. In the Europa League, they thrived, which was hardly a surprise, given Emery had four previous triumphs in the competition on his CV: three with Sevilla, one with Villarreal. 12 wins from 14 games took them to the final in Istanbul, where Freiburg were no match. By the time Morgan Rogers scored in the 58th minute, it was 3-0 and game over. That night in May, Villa won their first major trophy since the 1995/96 League Cup. “We played in a very serious way this year,” said Emery afterwards. “This final is the confirmation of how we are progressing.” The problem for Villa was that the cost of their success was rapidly increasing. With two prior fines handed down for breaching UEFA’s squad cost ratio (SCR) regulations, they knew they had to take action to comply. Cue a very hectic summer transfer window, during which the spine of the team was sold: Youri Tielemans to Manchester United, Ezri Konsa to Arsenal, Emi Martínez to Chelsea, Ollie Watkins to Al Hilal and, most notably, Morgan Rogers also to Chelsea for £117m - the all-time record fee paid for an English player. They reportedly spent more than £250m on replacements, including Johan Manzambi, who starred for Switzerland at the World Cup, striker Nicolas Jackson from Chelsea and Japan international goalkeeper Zion Suzuki. Emery’s new-look team took four games to score their first Premier League goal of the season and five to pick up their first Premier League win, against Tottenham just before the international break. But they are up and running in cup competitions after a 3-1 win victory against Coventry City in the Carabao Cup and a 3-2 win over Club Brugge in the Champions League league phase. There are signs the new team is beginning to gel - and if Emery can replicate anything close to last season’s success in spite of the wholesale changes, it could be one of his finest achievements yet. Having taken charge of more than 1,000 matches over the last 22 years, Unai Emery is one of the most experienced managers currently working in the Premier League. After a career as a midfielder, mostly playing in the second tier of Spanish football, the Spaniard had a pretty quick transition into management, having suffered a serious knee injury in his early 30s. He helped the now-defunct Lorca Deportiva gain promotion in 2004/05 and got Almería into La Liga for the first time in 2006/07, before an incredible eighth-place finish the following campaign. In 2008, his exploits saw him move on to Valencia, whom he guided to three straight third-place finishes from 2010 to 2012, before a forgettable six-month spell in Russia with Spartak Moscow. He returned to Spain in January 2013 and guided Sevilla to three-successive Europa League titles. Two years and seven trophies with Paris Saint-Germain followed, with Emery then trusted by the Arsenal board to become the successor to Arsène Wenger, which was, to an extent, a poisoned chalice. The Europa League king guided the Gunners to the final in 2019, where they were beaten by Chelsea in Baku, Azerbaijan, but he was unable to help them finish higher than fifth for the first time in four seasons. He was dismissed after 18 months in November 2019 and appointed by Villarreal in July 2020, with - you’ve guessed it - a fourth Europa League triumph 10 months later, by way of a penalty shoot-out win over Manchester United in Gdańsk, Poland. Emery turned down an approach by Newcastle United in November 2021, but came back to England to replace Steven Gerrard at Villa Park in October 2022. The 54-year-old - under contract until the summer of 2029 – reached 200 games in charge of Aston Villa last month and is the club’s longest-serving manager since Ron Saunders, who left in February 1982 after more than 350 games. Sky Sports journalist Patrick Rowe has explained how Aston Villa are likely to approach Saturday's game. "It is new personnel, but the same formation really. It looks to be a 4-4-2, with one of Emi Buendía or Johan Manzambi playing off the striker," Rowe told brentfordfc.com. "Boubacar Kamara, one of the best midfielders in the league, in my opinion, will likely be paired with João Gomes in midfield. John McGinn plays out on the right, but loves to cut in. Buendía also drifts infield from the left. "Do not be surprised to see one of Ibrahim Mbaye or Alejandro Garnacho featuring out wide, though. "The new-look backline could feature Aaron Wan-Bissaka or Matty Cash at right-back. Matteo Ruggeri, the new signing from Atlético Madrid, did very well at left-back last time out. Villa need him given the injury to Ian Maatsen." Last Premier League starting XI v Tottenham (4-2-3-1): Suzuki; Wan-Bissaka, Lindelöf, Mings, Ruggeri; Kamara, João Gomes; McGinn, Manzambi, Buendía; Jackson Craig Pawson will take charge of Brentford's Premier League away game against Aston Villa. Pawson has overseen three games across the Premier League and Carabao Cup so far this term, dishing out 11 yellow cards and zero reds. Brentford won two and drew one of the three games that the Sheffield referee had the whistle for last term. A first-half strike from Dango Ouattara saw 10-man Brentford secure a first-ever away victory against Aston Villa. The Burkina Faso forward rifled a fine finish into the top corner shortly after Kevin Schade had been sent off, before a resolute second-half display saw the Bees claim an historic win.
