title: The Suncor v. Boulder SUPCO climate case - The Highland County Press
content:
By William P. Barr
Former U.S. Attorney General
Real Clear Wire This is a lightly edited transcript of a keynote delivered by Former U.S. Attorney General William Barr at "The Constitutional Stakes in Suncor v. Boulder," a Civitas Institute symposium held October 1, 2026, at The University of Texas at Austin. I am going to jettison my prepared remarks based on what I heard discussed on the panels earlier. The speech I prepared covered several different elements of Suncor v. Boulder, including practical considerations of the possible consequences of a victory for Colorado, but I worry people will think that I am evading some of the legal issues. I don’t want that to happen, so I’m going to talk more about the legal issues than I’d planned. Suncor v. Boulder is one of approximately three dozen cases that are pending under state tort laws, nuisance cases, and other theories. States and municipalities are applying those laws to impose liability on American energy companies for the alleged global effects of fossil fuel production and use. That effort reflects the climate movement’s basic narrative, which is that climate change is the result of long-term greenhouse gases build up in the Earth’s atmosphere. Worldwide carbon gas emissions are increasing and accumulating, they claim, which is is causing climate change. It’s important to focus on the mechanism they claim is causing injury: the greenhouse gases in the Earth’s atmosphere. Some 90% of those gases come from outside the U.S. What precisely are they trying to regulate? Their focus is not on companies’ activity in Colorado; they’re not claiming that as the basis of liability. They are saying that these companies’ worldwide oil and gas production and sale contributed to and enabled worldwide emissions, which has caused the accumulation. Therefore, they claim, these companies are responsible for climate change and the weather that has now adversely affected Colorado. Damages will ultimately be tailored to Colorado, but the activity that they are saying is the basis of liability are things that these companies do in Texas, the Middle East, or anywhere else in the world: the production and sale of fossil fuel energy, even though these countries sometimes desperately need the energy supplied by the U.S. Some of the speakers earlier dismissed the idea of structural preemption in this case, but there’s no basis for dismissing it because it is inherent in the Constitution and in case law. Prior cases reflected the necessary rule in those situations, which is that when something is inherently interstate in nature, the rules applied to it have to be neutral federal rules. One state cannot apply its rules to another state’s detriment. The paradigmatic example is a large lake that borders more than one state. Any individual state does not have the right to exclusively set the rules that govern that lake. Also imagine an interstate miasma that hangs over Oklahoma and Texas. Texas wants to handle it one way, and Oklahoma another. Who decides when something is one physical phenomenon that’s inherently interstate? One suggestion is that interstate emissions have always been subject to state regulation, which is untrue. States can regulate and apply their laws to impose liability for activities in their state, but they cannot apply their laws to activities outside the state. There’s an exception if the adverse effect in the other state is directly intended and targeted, like a shooting-across-the-border, for example. But generally speaking, if Colorado doesn’t like the extent to which ExxonMobil’s activities are contributing to something that they think is harming them, they can’t sue ExxonMobil under their law for activities in Texas. That’s a basic legal principle. The law is not flexible on this. The Clean Air Act does not change that. What it does is preserve power for the states to regulate their own emission sources. States set air quality standards that apply to fixed emission sites within their own territory. This is a complex process whereby they coordinate with other states and the EPA to work out regional plans. At the end of the day, however, it’s no surprise that one state cannot direct another state or regulate another state’s emissions. There was a case between New York and Vermont, for example. A mill in one state was polluting the water in a way that affected the other. The other state sued in response under its own law, which isn’t legal. You have to sue under the law of the state where the mill that’s discharging the pollutant is located. That’s the rule. In the case of these current emission lawsuits, it’s obvious that some of these energy companies were producing an emissions-causing product and selling it to those who ultimately emitted it. But they’re not being sued for selling it; they’re being sued because they contributed to interstate and international emissions. A state, however, like Colorado in Suncor, does not have the authority to unilaterally decide that it’s going to apply its own law to those emissions. Extraterritoriality is another point that is obviously at stake in this case and reflects the same basic principle: a state generally cannot exercise its powers outside of its own territory. There is not very much wiggle room in that doctrine. I do think there’s foreign affairs preemption, but first, let’s be clear: we’re talking about preemption. The Constitution’s structure preempts it because no single state can regulate an interstate phenomenon that affects multiple states. That’s the Clean Air Act’s whole basis: to provide for the regulation of air that’s constantly moving among states, because that movement is inherently an interstate phenomenon. The Clean Air Act was Congress’s effort to have federal supervision and rules regarding interstate emissions, while also preserving some room for the state to regulate sources in the state. The state’s regulatory authority, however, comes only from the statute. The Clean Air Act only replaces what it replaces in federal common law. It doesn’t replace the basic precept inherent in the Constitution, that a state does not have the authority to make rules for other states. Under the Clean Air Act itself, it’s preempted as well. There is also foreign affairs preemption. Now, as some said earlier, there are interesting questions about where to draw the line on foreign affairs preemption. But it is not necessary here. In the last thirty years since they applied it in Garamendi, the Court has not developed this doctrine, but it envisions a two-pronged test. First, is the state doing something that you would traditionally expect them to do? Are they exercising the normal police powers that you would expect them to? Second, if the state’s claim to be doing this as part of their traditional authority is a good one, then the Court must balance that interest against the federal government’s policy. But here this is not an exercise of traditional state power, so the measure will be struck down because it will have more than an incidental effect on U.S. foreign policy. I can’t think of anything more intrusive into foreign policy than these states’ efforts to determine relative liability and responsibility for atmospheric greenhouse gases and the extent to which people can be found responsible for climate changes or injurious effects. Determining this liability must happen on the international level to have any meaning; otherwise, you’re playing whack-a-mole. You’re destroying American oil and gas companies with no effect on emissions because production and sale of oil and gas will just shift to other producers, like China and Russia. That’s exactly what will happen under this sort of regime, because the countries that have state-owned energy companies—Russia, China, and Iran—which cannot be sued. U.S. companies will be the only companies paying in this scheme, which will drive up prices nationwide. This isn’t a state setting the price just for fuel within the state or “we’re going to add four cents to the cost of gasoline that’s sold in our state,” it is a coordinated effort by multiple states to swarm the industry and jack up prices. They have said this publicly. Once the first case is upheld, everyone else will come in with new cases, and we’re off to the races. It will be difficult for these public companies to survive, which is why they claim this litigation threatens them with bankruptcy. This is what we’re doing to our own industry through this state litigation, which is also beyond these states’ Constitutional power. I can’t think of anything more intrusive on foreign affairs than this. We have a policy of trying to resolve these environmental issues internationally. People may not like the positions we take, but we attempt to resolve them through bilateral discussions. Environmentalists might not feel like we’re moving fast enough, but they can always vote against the president if they don’t like an administration’s policy or push to pass a law. That is what the climate movement did for many years; they tried to go through the democratic process and push for treaties and statutes but were never able to achieve the radical action they wanted. Their new strategy is to swarm the industry with these state and municipal cases. That approach runs afoul of U.S. foreign policy. We’re not dealing with tobacco or a discretionary product; we’re dealing with energy, the foundation of civilization. Homo sapiens have been walking the earth for 300,000 years, and for most of that time, our lives have been nasty, brutish, and short. That fate only changed 300 years ago, coincident with the beginning of the fossil-fuel-based Industrial Revolution. There is a chart in Alex Epstein’s Fossil Future (2022) that shows how humanity’s well-being, life expectancy, per capita income, and population growth all coincide with our increased use of fossil fuels. Until the Industrial Revolution, human beings relied on muscles, horses, a few windmills, and burning wood, dung, and charcoal for fuel. That’s what we relied on until coal, oil, and natural gas changed everything. Canadian environmental scientist Vaclav Smil, whose books show how dependent the world is on fossil fuels, thinks this idea that we can quickly eliminate or start drastically reducing the use of fossil fuels is an illusion. It is caused by the disconnect between the life of urban elites and the truth of what supporting our society requires: runways and flights and the fertilizers half the world depends on, which are made from natural gas and the tremendous amount of heat that process generates. Every price increase and curtailment of fossil fuels, without a good idea of economic and effective substitutes, comes at a huge cost. This is a decision we’re choosing to make. The states are playing in the wrong ballpark. They’re looking at this issue as though it’s a tort and asking how much damage was done, and how much the companies paid. But that issue of torts is not the issue the U.S. faces. But tort damages is not the issue that the U.S. or the world faces. The real issue is how do we sensibly try to reduce emissions without destroying our economies the way Germany has. That’s the way everyone else in the world is looking at it now. But the climate activists don’t want a national decision. They don’t want this question to go through the political process, where there will be a discussion of the pros and cons and benefits of fossil fuel and what it means to lose those benefits. Climate activists want the jury to decide how much companies have to pay out. We can’t go into the courtroom and point out that people will die if the energy prices rise because that’s not a defense in a tort case. But questions about consequences are questions we must raise, and that requires the political process. It also requires a locus of responsibility. We need people we can hold accountable for these decisions, rather than a bunch of municipal and state judges making individual decisions across the country that cumulatively destroy the American energy industry. And what will that destruction do? The market won’t disappear because there is no suitable energy substitute. People will still use petroleum and natural gas that will come from far less environmentally sensitive foreign suppliers. And all we will have succeeded in doing is destroying our own industry with no environmental benefit. That’s exactly why any sensible person agrees that these policies must be pursued through international agreements. Otherwise, we’re going to end up holding the bag. The Constitution is a sensible document; the structures it builds align with reasonable common sense. The idea that the Constitution would enable local courts to make independent judgments dealing with who pays for worldwide emissions is preposterous. That would require local juries making judgments on whether the Chinese and their thousands of coal plants, for example, bear more responsibility for emissions than ExxonMobil. This is not a question the courts are best suited to answer; it is a question of whether the democratic process works. If it doesn’t, people have a remedy. It’s certainly not a case for state courts. We need national rules and approaches. Is this the logical place to make these decisions? No, but it’s where the environmental movement likes to make policy. Federal courts don’t seem hospitable to these suits and that’s why they’re happening at the state and municipal courts. The litigants know that if they in the federal court system these cases will make their way to the Supreme Court, where all these conservatives are. So they need to find someplace else to pursue this agenda. I hope the Court takes a stand on this because it isn’t just a run-of-the-mill decision. This issue has been percolating for years. These are public companies. They need investments. We need to know that we can fulfill our commitments to provide natural gas to the Europeans, for example. We can’t have this morass of litigation around the country hanging over us while we’re moving forward.

title: Liverpool v Man City: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: BBC Sport examines some of the key themes before Sunday's match (16:30 BST), with Manchester City likely to face a hostile atmosphere away to Liverpool in their first game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. This promises to be a unique occasion in the rivalry between these clubs, and not only because it will be their first meeting since 2015 without either Jurgen Klopp or Pep Guardiola in the dugout. Liverpool and Manchester City have been the Premier League's two most successful clubs in recent years, but a question mark now hangs over many of City's achievements after an independent commission found the club guilty of breaching the league's financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18. City maintain their innocence and have appealed against the verdict. But if it is upheld, Liverpool supporters would be entitled to wonder whether some of English football's biggest prizes might otherwise have ended up at Anfield. Liverpool were runners-up to City in the league in 2014 and lost to them in the League Cup final two years later. Although the breaches they have been found guilty of happened before Klopp's side reached their peak, many of the players City signed between 2009 and 2018 helped deny the Reds the title in 2019 and 2022, when the Merseysiders finished second despite collecting more than 90 points. But for all the controversy surrounding the fixture, Liverpool's immediate concern is ending their wait for a first home league win under Andoni Iraola. That task has been complicated by injuries to top scorer Alexander Isak and the in-form Cody Gakpo on international duty, placing greater onus on Florian Wirtz to prove his worth. The 23-year-old has scored only one club goal since January but was on target in Germany's win over Serbia on 1 October. Wirtz has yet to fully convince since joining for a fee that could rise to £116m, but it is not for want of trying. He has covered an average of 11.9km per 90 minutes, the fourth-highest figure in the Premier League this season and ranks second for distance covered at high speed. Manager Enzo Maresca has rejected suggestions that Manchester City's achievements have been tainted by the guilty verdict. At Friday's news conference, Maresca said he "completely trusts" the club, bullishly insisting the right time to discuss the case would be "when we win the appeal". The Italian added his job was to manage the "noise" surrounding City and concentrate on the immediate task of winning Sunday's game. His chances of doing so have been boosted by the availability of Erling Haaland, who scored five goals in three games against Liverpool last season. The striker is fit despite being forced off during Norway's defeat by Portugal last weekend. Should Maresca maintain his perfect start with City, he would join an illustrious group of managers to win their first six Premier League matches in charge. His City predecessor Pep Guardiola achieved the feat in 2016, as did fellow Italian Carlo Ancelotti with Chelsea in 2009 and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after taking charge of Manchester United during the 2018-19 season. Those three were all making their debuts in the English top flight, unlike Maresca, whose first Premier League season came with Chelsea in 2024-25.

title: Hull City v Everton: Key stats and talking points - BBC
content: After their first setback of the season before the international break, Hull City will be hoping to get on track again when they welcome an unbeaten Everton team to the MKM Stadium on Sunday (14:00 BST). The Tigers were unable to recover from two early Newcastle United goals last time out, eventually losing 2-1 at St James' Park in what was their first league loss of the campaign. But they go into the weekend in eighth and with a solid foundation in place to keep clear of relegation trouble. Everton sit a place above Hull in seventh. David Moyes and his players have had a lot of noise to deal with off the pitch - it was confirmed on Friday that the club is up for sale - but on he field they've performed well, winning four and drawing three matches in all competitions so far. Keep it tight and play on the counter-attack. Hull's plan has been clear since their return to the top flight. Unfortunately for head coach Sergej Jakirovic, the blueprint is not compatible with being two goals down after seven minutes, as they were at Newcastle. They did at least respond well and gave themselves a chance thanks to Mohamed-Ali Cho's second-half goal. But it was too much of a deficit for the Tigers to tackle. In terms of approach, it would be a surprise if too much changed against Everton, with Hull's plan serving them well through the first four games. Jakirovic's side won't be desperate to get on the ball, that's for sure. So far this season, they rank 20th among Premier League teams for successful passes – Hull's total of 1,017 is 305 lower than Coventry City's 1,322, in 19th – and average possession, with 32.3%. Everton, their opponents this weekend, rank 17th in the latter category with 43.6%. They have also only completed 22 sequences of 10 or more passes, which is a league low. Their rate of 0.4 build-up attacks per 90 is also the lowest by a Premier League team in any season since 2018-19 (Cardiff City's 0.37 per game). Although some sales late in the transfer window left Everton without any depth in key positions, a number of different players have been able to step up and shine. Young midfielder Harrison Armstrong leads the Premier League for distance covered so far with 60.4km, while the return to fitness of Jarrad Branthwaite – he leads the league for blocks with 11 – has been key to Everton having the joint-best defensive record in the division going into the weekend. Branthwaite's presence also brings out the best in Blues captain James Tarkowski, who has started this campaign well after a tough end to 2025-26. The veteran centre-back has the best success rate of any player to contest 15 or more duels in the Premier League this season, with 83%. He is also the only defender to make 10 or more tackles and 10 or more interceptions, with 11 and 14 respectively. Tarkowski also has a goal and an assist for good measure. Most crucially, though, when Branthwaite and Tarkowski have been on the field together for the Toffees, improved results have followed. title: Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: BBC Sport examines some of the key themes before Sunday's match (14:00 BST), with Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner returning to face former club Crystal Palace. "If you can't beat 'em, join 'em." That seems to have been the approach of Glasner, who failed to win any of his five games against Forest as Palace boss before swapping Selhurst Park for the City Ground this summer. Palace's poor record in this fixture predates Glasner's appointment in 2024, with the Londoners winless in all 12 Premier League meetings. That is the most they have faced an opponent in the competition without winning, and likewise the most games Forest have played against one side without losing. A convincing case can be made that Glasner is the most successful manager in Palace's history. The Austrian led them to their first two major honours - the FA Cup in 2025 and the Conference League a year later. Some supporters may have been disappointed that he left to join a club who finished one place below Palace last season. However, owner Steve Parish has urged fans to give him a "fantastic reception" and ignore the "pantomime narratives". Glasner's successor, Pierre Sage, earned his first Premier League clean sheet in the draw against Leeds United last time out but has lost both of his top-flight home games. The Frenchman has chopped and changed so far, fielding 27 players in the league, a joint record by any Premier League team after five matches. Continuity will be needed if they are to climb the table. Nottingham Forest were one of four Premier League clubs - including Crystal Palace - who earned more points away than at home last season, and that trend has become even more pronounced this term. Forest have failed to score in all four of their league and cup games at the City Ground, but have drawn 2-2 at Liverpool and won 2-1 at Aston Villa. Including last season, they have scored at least twice in seven consecutive top-flight away matches, the longest such run in the club's history. One of the key players behind that sequence has been Morgan Gibbs-White. The 26-year-old played only 45 minutes during the international break, split between four substitute appearances for England, but is undoubtedly the talisman for his club. Gibbs-White has either scored or assisted in eight consecutive Premier League away games, one short of the record shared by Andy Cole, Robin van Persie and Erling Haaland.

title: Premier League today: How to watch Manchester United v Spurs, TV channels & live stream Saturday 10 October - The Guardian
content: How will Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options The sense of desperation will be strong as Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur arrive at Old Trafford with both teams in bad need of a win to change the narrative around their disappointing seasons so far. Anything less than three points would further increase the pressure on Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi, both of whom are fighting to prove they are the right people for their respective jobs. Saturday’s match could be pivotal. Spurs can take encouragement from the fact they have won four of their last six encounters with United in all competitions dating back to September 2024. Less positive is their run of four blanks in the five league matches they have played so far this season. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options. Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur have suffered many of the same problems to start the season. Both teams have conceded far too many goals and struggled for any sort of defensive foundation. The former have yet to keep a single clean sheet in five league games while the latter have kept just two. In midfield, Carrick and De Zerbi struggling for the right balance. Manchester United and Spurs both bought expensive new midfielders in the summer transfer window who have yet to settle into their new surroundings. Things haven’t been much better in the attacking third where Spurs have scored in just one of their five league games. For Manchester United, the likes of Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Bryan Mbeumo have yet to find top form. This match could be a catalyst, but it’s not clear for whom. title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort - The Guardian
content: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat Visitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest. But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best. As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of the Tobago Hotel and Tourism Association, says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have. “There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds. With that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the government agency Eteck, which manages and develops economic zones. Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas. Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point. Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago. “Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says. He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry. Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised. “The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels. Michelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist and director at the NGO SpeSeas, says more than 100 people submitted written objections to the Environmental Management Authority (EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments. After the adjustments, the EMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC, with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow. Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring. Cazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”. Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says. She adds that the trees provide shade and help protect the beach from coastal erosion, and their removal would harm one of Tobago’s most important turtle nesting sites. “At Back Bay, the shade keeps the sand cool,” she says, making it a choice for hawksbill turtles and leatherback turtles laying their eggs. Cazabon-Mannette says that sediment runoff from development could also threaten the unique coral reef that makes it a surfer’s paradise. The developer has promised to set up silt fences during construction to control sediment runoff, but “these things fail all the time”, Kenny says. When questioned about the concerns of environmentalists, John Aboud, chairman of Superior Hotels T&T, replied to the Guardian by forwarding the CEC, without further comment. While the EMA approval has been issued, final approvals from Tobago’s Town and Country Planning Division and the assembly, its legislative body, remain under review. Marriott International, the company reportedly in talks to manage the resort, says it is not involved in the proposed development at Rocky Point and that it has not executed any agreement with Superior Hotels for the site. The EMA and Eteck were also approached for comment. Brathwaite says that expecting a developer to make significant changes to designs after an environmental impact assessment is completed would be unrealistic. “There is a general resistance to making any modifications because they have already spent quite a lot of money.” He believes that once the EMA grants a CEC and the accompanying mitigation measures are followed, there should be no real concerns about its environmental impact. “The CEC codifies the conditions that have to be met … and the monitoring requirements scale with the likely risk and severity posed to the environment in which the activities are proposed to be carried out,” he says. “So they become progressively more stringent for areas that are more environmentally sensitive.” Yet many local people believe a development that needs so many mitigation measures, which they consider to carry extensive risks, is not the way forward for Tobago. The Caribbean Natural Resources Institute (Canari) has been advocating a different approach, called community-based tourism, in other areas of Tobago, such as Speyside, about an hour’s drive north of Rocky Point. Dylis McDonald, Canari’s senior technical officer, says projects such as the one at Speyside are usually small-scale and rooted in community members’ own vision for their future. “In the community-based tourism space, very often conservation, restoration and protection are core to what the enterprises are doing,” she says. “There is a particular type of ownership and understanding and connection to the areas where those activities are implemented.” Campaigners and experts acknowledge that while small hotels succeed in Tobago, other small-scale eco-tourism sites may still not consistently provide steady income. Turtle nesting patrols, for instance, employ people to protect the hatchling turtles and eggs, but it is seasonal work that offers only a stipend when funds are available. Yet, Kenny says, a development that is in harmony with nature and a sustainable business model is possible. “You can have your cake and eat it, too.”

title: New Zealand v Australia: All Blacks power past Wallabies 50-19 to retain Bledisloe Cup - BBC
content: Tries: Lakai, Vaai, Roigard, Taylor, Carter, Moorby, Jordan Cons: McKenzie (6) Pens: McKenzie New Zealand retained the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year as they powered past Australia to extend their remarkable unbeaten run at Eden Park. The All Blacks have not lost at the venue since 1994, with a dominant second-half display increasing their unbeaten run in Auckland to 54 Tests. Australia remained in touch at half-time at 17-14 down but New Zealand blew the visitors away after the break, scoring five tries. Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan all scored as fly-half Damian McKenzie kicked 15 points to help the All Blacks retain the trophy which is contested annually between the two nations. Victory halted a three-match losing streak for the All Blacks after the 3-1 series defeat by world champions South Africa this summer. Defeat for the Wallabies was their first since head coach Les Kiss succeeded Joe Schmidt in July, ending their six-game unbeaten run. Australia were looking for their first win at Eden Park since 1986 and went ahead after controlling the early stages through full-back Tom Wright's try. New Zealand responded strongly, and inspired by scrum-half Roigard's searching kicks, turned the match around with tries from Lakai and Vaa'i. Wallabies captain Harry Wilson scored a try to keep New Zealand at arm's length, but the All Blacks moved through the gears in the second half. Roigard grabbed a try for himself shortly after the break, before Taylor, Carter, Moorby and Jordan went over as Australia struggled to hold back the hosts' waves of attack. Josh Nasser added a late try for the visitors, but the match was well beyond their reach by that point. The second match of the two-Test series takes place in Sydney at the Accor Stadium on 17 October. A feast of fast ruck ball, superior box-kick chasing, and the ability to snuff out the few dangerous assaults the Wallabies mustered carried the All Blacks to a thumping 50–19 win that retained the Bledisloe Cup and extended their run of Eden Park victories to 54 since 1995. Needing to stop their three-game losing run against South Africa, the All Blacks turned it on in a powerful second half that all but shut the Australians out. Flanker Peter Lakai and No.8 Wallace Sititi's work in the loose and in support play was matched by an outstanding display from blindside flanker Tupou Vaa’i. A constant support player, and superb in securing kicks ahead, he gave the side genuine impetus time after time. So too did returning lock Scott Barrett, in his 90th Test. He was relentless in charging into the Wallaby defenders and fully vindicated the selectors' recall. He brought experience that demonstrated his value to the side. Lock Josh Lord came back after early Australian disruption of the All Blacks’ lineout to add quality and help build the side's momentum. First five-eighths Damian McKenzie proved himself consistently, and his speedy breaks frustrated Australia early. His five-eighths partner, Jordie Barrett, was also ever present, chasing kicks ahead while he and centre Quinn Tupaea continue to build a meaningful midfield partnership. But again, the ability of halfback Cam Roigard to make the right decisions at the right times was another factor in the win. His box kicks were precise, far better than rival Ryan Lonergan's. The All Blacks were rewarded thirty minutes from the end when the lineout maul came up trumps after lock Josh Lord’s take. Backs joined the maul to add momentum, and after hooker Codie Taylor was tackled short of the line, halfback Cam Roigard took his chance and scored around the base. Four minutes later, the All Blacks pack was rampant, with destructive hand-to-hand work punching the ball forward, and Taylor found the final gap to charge and help extend the lead to 31-14. That broke the Australian resolve, and while they picked up a late try from replacement hooker Josh Nasser, it was countered by a last-gasp try from winger Will Jordan after a backline passing error by Australia, which allowed Jordan to toe the ball ahead to bring up the half-century. Early penalties conceded by Tupaea and captain Codie Taylor allowed Australia to apply early pressure through lineout mauls. After Lord was caught offside, Australia moved the ball with blind-side wing Max Jorgenson joining the line to create a gap, allowing fullback Tom Wright to ease through and open the scoring. Beauden Barrett kicked the ball dead from the restart, but any advantage Australia might have had from the midfield scrum was negated when first five-eighths Ben Donaldson kicked the ball out on the full. Roigard kicked into the box from the lineout, and, in changed form, chasing those kicks, the All Blacks secured the ball through Jordie Barrett; the ball was spun to McKenzie, who raced into a gap and split the Australians. When he needed to pass wide, Lakai was the man on the spot to secure the All Blacks’ try in response after 11 minutes. Four minutes later, McKenzie found another gap and, this time linked with Sititi; after a series of rucks Vaa’i scored. Soon after, Jordan broke brilliantly through midfield, but he couldn’t find All Black hands out wide, and the ball went into touch. McKenzie lifted New Zealand to 17 points with a 33rd-minute penalty goal. But three minutes before the break, Australia got back in touch after a lineout near the All Blacks’ 22m area; Donaldson took a gap and found No.8 Harry Wilson, perfectly placed in support and score handy to the posts, and Australia went to the break 14-17 down. In the final analysis, this was an emphatic statement by the All Blacks and was a positive result for the style of rugby they are attempting to develop. New Zealand: 50 (Peter Lakai, Tupuo Vaa’i, Cameron Roigard, Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby, Will Jordan tries; Damian McKenzie 6 con, pen) Australia: 19 (Tom Wright, Harry Wilson, Josh Nasser tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 con). HT: 17-14

title: Liverpool v Manchester City: Team news - Liverpool FC
content: Liverpool must make at least two changes for their hosting of Manchester City on Sunday, with Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak sidelined. The forward pair suffered injuries during the international break that have ruled them out of the Premier League fixture at Anfield. But Jeremy Jacquet, who missed France's win over Belgium at the start of the week, is set to be available. Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola told reporters: "Cody has an ankle injury. He has had some before in his career and it's a matter of him dealing with the pain because when you twist your ankle... it was a really bad tackle, I think. "He is doing things individually but [he is] not ready for Sunday. "And Alex has a thigh injury. It's a small injury but it's a muscle injury. The same [as Gakpo], whenever he feels ready. "They both don't look like long term – we will be analysing day to day. But they are not going to arrive on Sunday." With Isak and Gakpo out, Iraola was asked about his options in the final third of the pitch. He said: "Even before, we don't have Hugo Ekitike, who is another very good striker that I'm looking forward to having available also. "We don't have Hugo, we don't have Alex. We will maybe recover Fede Chiesa but he hasn't played any minutes. He is recovering from an injury but he has been doing a good job in the international break, he has been training with the small group we had. "A full No.9, it's true that we probably only have [Lewis] Koumas right now, but we have some other options. We have some wingers that have played up front in other teams. "I think we will put an XI with a level enough to compete for that game." Inside Training: Liverpool squad return ahead of Manchester City match! Bradley Barcola, five matches into his Liverpool career, is a winger with previous experience of playing in a central attacking role. "He is a top player for us. I think he can play in any position up front," said Iraola. "He probably has played more as a left winger but has played a little bit as a striker, has played even more as a right winger. I think he can cover the three positions up front." As well as Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni are long-term absentees for the hosts. In terms of the visitors, City boss Enzo Maresca declared Erling Haaland to be fit for the game. The striker had been withdrawn, as a precaution, during Norway's final match of the international window last Sunday. Maresca reported of Haaland's availability: "He's good. He went to Marbella, [had] two, three days off, played golf, recovery. Phil Foden cannot feature on Merseyside, however, as he is currently suspended. A fitness issue saw Nico O'Reilly withdraw from the England squad midway through the international break. title: Premier League today: How to watch Arsenal v Leeds United, TV channels & live stream Saturday 10 October - The Guardian
content: How will Arsenal and Leeds United fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Three points is all that separates Arsenal and Leeds United as the Premier League returns after a three-week international break, with the latter one of the surprise packages of the season so far. Unlike Arsenal, Leeds have yet to lose a league game this season. Daniel Farke’s team have earned a reputation for being difficult to beat and have the quality to cause an upset in north London this weekend. Mikel Arteta’s champions have had a long time to simmer on their shocking 3-0 defeat to Brighton in their final outing before the international break. The Gunners’ fans expect a response from their team to keep their title defense on track. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. Until their defeat at the Amex Stadium, Arsenal’s title defense had started perfectly. Four wins from four had Arteta’s side setting the pace once again at the top of the Premier League table. Brighton, however, may have exposed some weaknesses in the Gunners in a way that others could attempt to replicate. Like Brighton, Leeds are dangerous in quick transition. They currently rank top for interceptions per 90 minutes in the Premier League, highlighting their determination to win the ball high up the pitch as often as possible. Injuries suffered by Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Christos Tzolis over the international break could also be a problem. This is where Arsenal’s squad depth will be tested – although it should be noted Leeds haven’t beaten the north London outfit in the Premier League since 2003. Player to watch: Bukayo Saka, Arsenal – The right winger returns to club duty on the back of bagging a brace for England in their 7-0 demolition of Croatia. With question marks over the fitness of Havertz and Odegaard, Saka could be even more crucial for Arsenal.

I'm just going to come out and say it: I've enjoyed the international break – there, I've done it and admitted this to myself. By the way, when I mean enjoyed it, I haven't watched one England game… or any other international fixture. It just feels like the calm before the storm: nine games in thirty days and it all starts today. Knowing that, it was easy to not want the next fixture to come too quickly because it's going to be relentless. By the way, on this, I'd love to be a young'un with no responsibilities. I thought it was fun travelling the length of the country watching Reidy's side, but if you're at the right age with nothing to worry about and disposable cash, the next couple of months are going to be great. What it also means, however, is that we could do with setting the tone for the run ahead. I'm sure the mantra of taking one game at a time will be a thing, but it would be very useful to kick off this run with a result today, and that's not going to be an easy task. We'll come onto Brighton in a moment, but as international breaks go, it hasn't been our most productive on the face of it. I write this ahead of Le Bris' press conference, and everyone will be eager to hear what the official line is on Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey from the mouth of our manager, as well as rumours that Noah Sadiki and Wilson Isidor picked up knocks. Last season we had a very clear target of collecting forty points as quickly as possible, and a minimum requirement is to stay on a ratio of no worse than roughly one point per game. Should we lose today, we'll be slipping behind and building pressure to get that back on track. Now on to high-flying Brighton, who have carried on the momentum of qualifying for a European competition for a second time in four years, despite losing their last two games of the season. It was a fantastic achievement, which came at the end of Fabian Hürzeler's second season as manager, at the ripe old age of 33. Brighton once again pulled an appointment out of their data-driven hat to pull off another coup. This is especially true considering that former manager Roberto De Zerbi is languishing at the foot of the table with Spurs, while Brighton sit third, the usual suspects in the top two. On paper they roughly spent the amount they recouped with outgoing transfers, and got off to a cracking start by thumping Aston Villa 4-0 on the opening day. An unfortunate 4-3 defeat at Stamford Bridge and a disappointing draw at home to Leeds followed, but they then went to Coventry and won 5-0 and backed it up with the result of the season when they beat Arsenal 3-0 on home soil. They are shaping up for another impressive season down on the south coast, but time will tell if the result against Coventry was as good as it looks, and their other result on the road ended in defeat. Combine that with our performances before the break and knowing how good we can be at home, and we should still be confident. title: Here’s What Happened At The 2026 All Things Go Music Festival - V Magazine
content: V attended the renowned women-led festival’s original location for a third year in a row V attended the renowned women-led festival’s original location for a third year in a row Since its inception more than a decade ago, All Things Go Music Festival has stayed remarkably true to its mission – uplifting women and LGBTQ+ artists – while keeping music front and center. Amidst a myriad of high-profile music festivals that often feel more synonymous with a photo op or an aesthetic than the artists taking the stage themselves, All Things Go has fostered a culture that places the focus on talent, inclusivity, and community. Though the festival lineup historically tends to skew indie-pop, this year featured a more diverse range of sounds and genres, with more than 45 artists across two stages and three days. V returned to the beloved festival’s original location, now held at Merriweather Post Pavilion, to catch an incredible lineup full of established icons, rising stars, and V alums. Australian EDM artist Ninajirachi delivered an electrifying performance at the Chrysalis Stage on Friday afternoon, where her distinct, self-taught production skills were on full display. Fresh off her breakthrough album I Love My Computer, her DJ set evoked a sense of fun-loving nostalgia with standout tracks like “iPod Touch,” as infectious energy coursed through the crowd. V161 cover star Slayyyter, once an electro-pop cult favorite, has spent 10 years working toward her big break. With WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA, the world has finally caught on. That excitement and energy were evident at All Things Go, where the crowd was largely made up of longtime Slayyyter listeners. Performing hits like “CRANK,” the experimental artist had every member of the audience on their feet. But it was her encore—her latest infectiously catchy hit “brand new chanel$,” followed by its predecessor, “BEAT UP CHANEL$”—that solidified Slayyyter’s status as pop’s next big thing, on par with some of her own personal heroes. “Third time’s a charm!” Ethel Cain affectionately exclaimed to the crowd as she returned to the All Things Go Pavilion Stage (she graced the same stage in 2023 and the Chrysalis Stage in 2024). This year’s performance, however, marked an important milestone for the V141 cover star. After 107 shows over the course of nearly a year and a half, she took her final bow on her Willoughby Tucker Forever Tour, and the finale did not disappoint. With a setlist featuring some of Cain’s biggest pop heavy-hitters (“Crush,” “Dust Bowl,” “American Teenager”) and most devastating stripped-back ballads (“Nettles,” “Hard Times”), she showcased her range and vocal prowess, which somehow seem to reach new heights with every show. Another returning act, MUNA took the stage Saturday to a warm reception. As four-time All Things Go performers, the trio are seasoned veterans by now. Despite the upbeat nature of their latest album, DANCING ON THE WALL, the band brought a distinct tenderness to their performance, reminding audiences of their deep friendship and long history together, which dates back to their college days at the University of Southern California. This was especially evident in a standout moment when, sandwiched between classic hits like “Silk Chiffon” and “I Know A Place,” MUNA threw in “Crying On The Bathroom Floor,” a deep cut from the band’s debut album, About U. V159 cover star Zara Larsson delivered perhaps the set with the most star power of the weekend during Saturday night’s closing slot at the Chrysalis Stage. After toeing the line between global commercial success and Swedish pop stardom with a small-yet-loyal following for nearly two decades, Larsson has officially broken through to reach massive superstardom with her fifth studio album, Midnight Sun. Her setlist was chock-full of bangers, from older hits like “Symphony,” “Ruin My Life,” and “Never Forget You” to the tracks that have defined the last few years, including “Stateside,” “Eurosummer,” and the titular “Midnight Sun.” Complete with her unmatched vocals, incredible dancing, and several crowd-favorite moments (selecting a lucky fan to perform the “Lush Life” dance alongside her; audience members imitating her airlifted dolphin pose), Larsson delivered a memorable evening and then some. Despite taking the Chrysalis Stage at 12:30 p.m. on a rainy Sunday, Trousdale undeniably delivered one of the most striking sets at All Things Go. The trio seamlessly blended country and indie-pop with their addictive harmonies, leaving fans mesmerized by performances of songs including “Secondhand Smoke,” “Wouldn’t Come Back,” and “If I’m Honest.” If their own catalog wasn’t proof enough of Trousdale’s collective status as vocal and instrumental powerhouses, the group even pulled off the difficult feat of covering Fleetwood Mac’s “The Chain.” From the first notes of her piercing breakup anthem “Savannah,” it was clear Jensen McRae was the perfect act to continue the moody atmosphere set by Trousdale, albeit from underneath the pavilion. Between “Novelty” and “Massachusetts,” McRae chronicles the demise of a situationship like no one else. Coupled with her incredibly unique voice and lovably awkward demeanor, her songwriting makes her a captivating presence onstage. Fresh off the release of her eighth studio album, Popstar, V93 cover star Tinashe is re-establishing herself as a force to be reckoned with. She made the most of an hourlong set at All Things Go, with the first half devoted to performing her catalog and the second to showcasing her innovative hyperpop DJ skills. With remarkable visuals, dancing, and stage presence, Tinashe is proving herself to be more than an artist with a handful of breakout hits—she is reaching new heights in the eyes of critics and audiences alike. The notoriously prestigious Pitchfork recently rated Popstar a 9.0, calling it “the best pop album of the year.” V alum Remi Wolf wasn’t initially supposed to play All Things Go this year. Though she appeared on the Chrysalis Stage in 2023, she was a last-minute addition to the 2026 lineup, stepping in for a brief, 30-minute slot to fill in for Sienna Spiro. The unplanned performance marked Wolf’s first live show in over a year as she prepares to release her third studio album, Mud, due October 9. The performance effectively served as a sneak peek at the album and its new era, featuring lead singles “Bottle” and “Twiggy,” along with the live debuts of “I Won’t Cry” and the unreleased tracks “Champagne” and “Covered In Mud.” In a fun, unexpected moment, Wolf finished with a new variation of her hit track “Soup” to match the sonic evolution of her latest project. title: Vietnam’s V Studios Seals Multiple Deals On ‘Red Woman’ Including Sales To North America & Japan - Deadline
content:
EXCLUSIVE: V Studios, the Vietnamese production arm of Korean exhibitor CJ CGV, has closed multiple deals on supernatural fantasy Red Woman, including sales to NewGates Corporation for Japan and Mockingbird Pictures for the US and Canada. The film, which is V Studios’ first fully in-house produced feature, has also gone to Infinity Entertainment for Australia & New Zealand; NK Contents for South Korea; and Westec Media for Cambodia. V Studios, which was previously known as V Pictures and launched here at Busan two years ago, also handles international sales for a slate of films it has invested in, as well as third-party titles. Since launch, the company has handled films including horror hits Ma Da: The Drowning Spirit, The Corpse and The Corpse 2. Starring Minh Hang, Red Woman reimagines a figure from Vietnamese folk history, the eponymous and elusive ‘Red Woman’, a character that has primarily existed through Vietnamese oral culture and collective memory. Directed by Jack Carry On, the film is fully produced by V Studios with Tam Tuong on board as executive producer. The film marks Minh Hang’s return to cinema after a three-year hiatus, following previous theatrical titles including Sweet Trap and Sister Sister 2. She also starred in Naked Truth (2022), which was streamed in Southeast Asia by Netflix. The cast also includes Rima Thanh Vy (Furies), Nhat Kim Anh (The Musician At The Dragon Citadel), Khuong Le (Meet Me At The Eclipse), Phat La and Dai Nghia. Theatrical release in Vietnam is scheduled for November 27, 2026, followed by an international rollout. V Studios said: “For generations, Vietnamese children have grown up hearing warnings about ‘Red Woman’ – a mysterious woman said to take children away if they wandered too far or disobeyed their parents. Yet unlike many established figures in Asian mythology, Red Woman has no definitive appearance, mythology or widely accepted origin story. That absence gives the filmmakers an unusual opportunity: to transform a familiar cultural fear into an entirely original cinematic mythology. “At the heart of Red Woman is a deceptively universal proposition: What would you be willing to sacrifice to get the one thing you desire most? When people reach the deepest point of desperation, resentment or longing, Red Woman appears. Possessing seemingly limitless powers, she offers them the one wish they have always wanted fulfilled. But every miracle carries a price.” Vietnamese genre cinema has recently been on a roll with a string of hits including Crimson Snout (Quy Cau), Ma Da: The Drowning and The Sisters (Cam) demonstrating local audiences’ appetite for stories drawing on folk beliefs and culturally specific supernatural imagery. title: Arsenal v Leeds Match Preview: Team News, Predicted Lineup and Score Prediction - Yahoo Sports
content: Arsenal finally return to Premier League action on Saturday lunchtime when they welcome unbeaten Leeds United to the Emirates Stadium. The Gunners went into the extended international break on the back of a painful 3-0 defeat at Brighton, which ended their perfect start to the season and left them second in the table. Leeds, meanwhile, have quietly made an excellent start. Daniel Farke's side sit just three points behind Arsenal after five matches and are yet to lose in the league, while conceding only three goals. That should ensure there is no room for complacency from Mikel Arteta's players after what happened at the Amex. The international break created several fresh concerns, although there has also been some welcome news for Arteta. According to Arsenal's official team news update, Christos Tzolis will miss the game with a muscle injury and is expected to be out for a few weeks. Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa are set to be assessed before the match, while Declan Rice also needs careful management following his heavy workload. There is better news defensively. Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie have all returned to training. With Tzolis missing and Havertz doubtful, this could be Viktor Gyokeres' opportunity to lead the attack. The Swede returns from an excellent international break in which he made Nations League history, having again demonstrated that he will score when a team plays to his strengths. Leeds are without some key players ahead of the Arsenal Match too. Predicted Arsenal lineup:Raya; Timber, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard; Saka, Eze; Gyokeres. Arsenal had looked in control of their season before that afternoon, but the 3-0 loss was a reminder that simply turning up is never enough in the Premier League. With Liverpool away coming next, dropping more points at home would immediately increase the pressure. I expect Leeds to make Arsenal work for it and their unbeaten record suggests they are unlikely to collapse easily. That’s a bit deceptive because he already has three full-distance races counting for his total, so winning the series would be a stretch, but a top finish will certainly offer a lucrative payday for Hanson. title: How I Got Here: Olena V. Ripnick-O’Farrell ’14 - Columbia Law School
content: Olena V. Ripnick-O'Farrell ’14 is global copyright counsel at ByteDance, a multinational technology company that develops AI models and operates global platforms, including TikTok, that cut across commerce, content, entertainment, and enterprise. I counsel at the intersection of copyright and AI, which means I think about novel issues of copyright law day in and day out. It’s my dream job—focusing solely on copyright is what I’ve always wanted to do in my legal career. My role requires agility, and, much like myself, it doesn’t fit neatly into any box. I’m a U.S. copyright law expert with a deep knowledge of EU and U.K. copyright law, and my practice over the past decade has been a tapestry of litigation, product counseling, and commercial transactions. At ByteDance, I blend substantive knowledge with practical experience to support the development of our AI models and advise internal stakeholders on novel and complex issues of copyright law. I couldn’t think of a role better suited for me. My brain seeks novelty while at the same time craving complexity and deep thinking, and grappling with legal questions for which there are no clear answers and counseling across multiple workstreams brings me joy. I’m on an all-female team for the first time in my legal career, and my teammates are some of the sharpest attorneys I’ve ever worked with. I’m so proud to be a part of this group. This is also the first time in my career where my practice is focused purely on copyright. It’s rare for an IP attorney to be able to specialize like this, and, like most, my previous practice included trademark and right of publicity. I’m indebted to Jeff Cunard, a former Debevoise partner with whom I remain in touch, for enabling me to develop my copyright practice as an associate. If he hadn’t supported me in doing so, the doors that opened and led me to my current role would have remained firmly shut. Professor Jane Ginsburg. I fell in love with copyright law on the very first day of her introductory copyright course. Jane is incredibly knowledgeable and passionate about this subject, and she’s so thoughtful in considering these complex issues. After taking this course, I ended up taking every copyright-related course that Columbia Law offered—including Jane’s elective on international copyright law, which remains relevant in my practice today—and I also served as her research assistant. One of the most exciting things about copyright law is that there aren’t many bright-line rules or clear-cut answers. It’s an evolving space, and the issues I advise on are constantly on my mind, even outside of working hours. Some of my best thinking happens when I’m not at my desk, often on the weekends or when I’m outdoors. To be honest, my passion for this subject probably exceeds what is healthy or typical, but I’m fine with that. I’ve always been interested in legal issues relating to gender equality and the LGBTQ+ community. During my time at the Law School, I was on the staff of the Columbia Journal of Gender and Law, and I served as the vice president of Columbia OutLaws. I also held internships with Immigration Equality and the ACLU’s LGBTQ & HIV Project. Visibility matters. I’m a queer, neurodivergent woman from a rural town in the Catskills. I’ve never had anyone like me to look up to as I have navigated my legal career. Neurodivergence—along with mental health conditions and other disabilities—remains highly stigmatized in the legal profession. There’s an irony here because many neurodivergent traits, such as hyperfocus under pressure, pattern recognition and issue spotting, rules-based system-oriented thinking, and creative problem solving, are significant strengths in practicing law. Each day I choose to be open about my identity, knowing the risk that this entails. I want things to be even a little bit less challenging for those who come next, and my advocacy comes in many forms. I exist openly. I educate others about neurodiversity and neuroinclusive best practices. I assist neurodivergent individuals in navigating the ADA [Americans with Disabilities Act] accommodation process, which can be overwhelming for those who struggle with executive function. And I regularly counsel neurodivergent law students and associates navigating the legal profession. First, keep going. Persevere. Ask for feedback, and learn from your mistakes. Grit and a growth mindset are the most important traits you can develop in any profession. Second, your health is your wealth. You must prioritize it over everything else because no one else will. This perspective is critical, and it’s one that I wish I had had earlier on in my career. title: What’s New in New Source Review? EPA’s Title V Rule Adds to a Growing List of NSR Developments - JDSupra
content:
Generally speaking, the CAA’s Title V Operating Permit program is a vehicle to compile and assure compliance with “applicable requirements” that other CAA programs impose on the source; it is not an opportunity to substantively reconsider the requirements themselves. That distinction is important because Title V has unique federal oversight tools that can disrupt permitting, including mechanisms for EPA to object to the issuance of a facility’s state-issued Title V operating permit and cause the permit to be modified, revoked, or terminated. Title V also establishes a related process for members of the public to petition EPA for such an objection, with exceptionally tight deadlines that can quickly force an EPA response. EPA’s final rule codifies an approach the agency had developed in a pair of Title V orders, Hunter and Big River Steel, both issued in October 2017. Under that approach, when an NSR permit is issued subject to requirements for public notice, opportunity for public comment, and opportunity for judicial review, the resulting terms and conditions are the NSR-related “applicable requirements” under Title V and cannot be revisited during the Title V permitting process. That principle extends to NSR permit content, such as Best Available Control Technology (BACT) determinations, and whether major or minor NSR applies. Limited Title V review remains available where NSR requirements have not been conclusively established, including where no NSR permit was issued, or the requisite opportunities for public participation and judicial review were not available. Separately, but also notably, the final rule also clarifies that the General Duty Clause of CAA Section 112(r)(1) is not an “applicable requirement” according to EPA’s statutory interpretation of Title V. However, accident-prevention requirements under CAA Section 112(r)(7) remain subject to Title V’s definition of “applicable requirements.” The Title V final rule on “applicable requirements” is the latest in a series of recent developments related to NSR. The changes and proposed changes are particularly relevant to companies planning to develop data centers, onsite generation, or to undertake other major capital projects, where air permitting requirements can often affect construction schedules. EPA guidance and rulemakings, federal court decisions, pending legislation, and enforcement litigation are addressing when NSR applies, how sources calculate emissions, when construction may begin, and how NSR disputes should be resolved: NSR developments are not limited to EPA. In Congress, several pieces of proposed legislation would alter aspects of NSR permitting. For example, the House Energy and Commerce Committee has reported out: In the courts, NSR enforcement litigation remains consequential. Earlier this year in United States v. EES Coke Battery, LLC, the Eastern District of Michigan imposed a $100 million civil penalty and injunctive relief for NSR violations, and held not just the plant owner liable, but also several other affiliated entities liable as “operators” due to the high degree of control they exhibited over the facility. United States v. EES Coke Battery, LLC, 820 F. Supp. 3d 600 (E.D. Mich. 2026). Given the stakes for project timing and the highly fluid NSR landscape, companies must consider how these recent and ongoing developments affect applicability analyses, construction sequencing, offset acquisition, compliance documentation, and overall air permitting strategy. And these relatively recent developments capture only part of the broader range of NSR issues that may arise, including source-determination questions such as common control and adjacency, project aggregation and “circumvention,” and the scope of what constitutes a major modification. In the case of EPA’s recent rule clarifying “applicable requirements” under Title V, a principal benefit is that it formally limits opportunities to use the Title V process as a “second bite at the apple” for NSR determinations—some of which, as in Hunter, may be decades old. At the same time, the rule does not eliminate other avenues to challenge or enforce NSR requirements. By expressly limiting the extent to which underlying NSR determinations can later be revisited through Title V, the rule may instead place greater importance on strategic decisions made during the initial preconstruction permitting process, when public participation, agency review, and potential litigation can have immediate consequences for project schedules. Companies planning new facilities or modifications to existing ones should therefore consider not only whether and how NSR applies, but also how best to develop a defensible permitting record at the outset.
